Judgment is for Us" (13:40), and "You are only a warner, and Allah is the Trustee of All Affairs" (11:12). ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah reported that Ibn ʿAbbās explained the verse this way: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ longed for all people to believe and follow the guidance he brought, and Allah informed him that only those for whom He had decreed happiness from the first would believe, and only those for whom He had decreed it would go astray.

The verse is a comfort to the Prophet ﷺ. Some disbelievers were so vain, arrogant and set in their opinions that even after recognising the truth they refused it and would not listen to it or look at the plainest proofs, so his efforts to reform and win them would bear no fruit, and for them it made no difference whether he tried or not. The next verse gives the reason: their hearts and ears were sealed and their eyes covered, so every avenue of knowing and understanding was shut, and no change could be expected from them.

Two limits must be kept in mind. First, "they will never believe" is said specifically about those disbelievers who refused to listen to the Prophet ﷺ and who, as Allah knew, would die in disbelief. It is not a statement about disbelievers in general, for many of them later accepted Islam. Second, the verse says it is the same "for them". It is not the same for the Prophet ﷺ. He earns his reward in any case for bringing Allah's message to people and for his effort to teach and reform them, which is why not one verse in the Qur'an tells him to stop calling even such people to Islam. From this it follows that whoever strives to spread the word of Allah and improve his fellow human beings is always rewarded for the work, even when it has no visible effect.

### The two camps

In the Prophet's ﷺ time there were two distinct groups among those who rejected the Qur'an. One came out in open hostility and denial, and the Qur'an calls them kāfirūn. The other, out of moral weakness and greed, lacked even the courage to speak its mind. They tried to convince the Muslims that they believed in the Qur'an and its teachings, that they were as good Muslims as anyone and would stand with the Muslims against the disbelievers, while nursing denial in their hearts and assuring the disbelievers, when alone with them, that they had nothing to do with Islam and mixed with the Muslims only to deceive them and spy on them. The Qur'an names them munāfiqūn, hypocrites. Seen whole, the opening of the surah sets out guidance and then sorts people into two kinds by their response to it: those who choose to follow it, the believers or the mindful, and those who reject it or swerve from it, the disbelievers or the hypocrites. The first kind are the people whose path is asked for at the end of al-Fātiḥah, the path of those Allah has favoured, and the second kind are those whose path refuge is sought from, those who earned anger and those who went astray.

A basic principle follows from this teaching. Any division of mankind into groups, if it is to mean anything, must rest on differences of principle, not on birth, race, colour, geography or language. The Qur'an gives a clear verdict: "He is the One Who created you, yet some of you are disbelievers while some are believers" (64:2).

### Why a clear call can fail

If a person closes his eyes he cannot see, and if he blocks his ears he cannot hear. However clear the call of truth, it can be understood and accepted only by someone who opens his mind to it. The silent call present in the universe, and its spoken form on the tongue of the preacher of Allah's word, cannot touch closed minds. The call of truth in its pure form rests on reality and agrees with human nature, and no one who hears it with an open mind can fail to recognise it. But where a society is rigidly bound by old conventions, people care less about opening their minds to divine realities than about protecting the vested interests of the existing system. The preacher, as Allah's envoy, neither represents nor supports the conventional structures of society, and his call, being new and unfamiliar, looks like a threat to people's material security. However much he urges them to submit to Allah's will, they baulk, because submitting would mean demolishing the world they have built for themselves. It is also hard for him to reach highly placed people, who fear that following an "insignificant" man will diminish their own glory. The two greatest obstacles to his success are worldliness and arrogance, and it is these states of mind, which stop people from accepting the truth, that the Qur'an calls seals on hearts.

### Bounty and justice

From the start of the surah up to this point the verses allude to the Lord's bounty and gentleness with His intimates and friends. This verse alludes to His severity and justice toward strangers and enemies. Allah has both bounty and justice. When He acts with justice it is fitting, and when He is bounteous it suits Him. Not everything that fits justice suits bounty, but everything that suits bounty fits justice. One person He calls toward bounty, by His decree. Another He drives toward justice, by His will. The good news is that bounty rules over justice: justice falls silent before bounty, and the fruit of bounty is felicity and triumph while the outcome of justice is wretchedness and estrangement. Both are done deeds. The Prophet ﷺ said that the Pen has already dried over everything that is to happen until the Resurrection. The decree has no beginning, and the work is finished. When someone's lot has set him down, his eagerness will not lift him up. The master of the path prayed in this spirit: O Allah, what comes of what You do not want, and when does he come whom You have not called? What good is water to ground that was never sown, or an answer to one who is unworthy? What does bitter water gain from sweet water beside it, or the thorn from the rose's scent next to it? The apportioning has gone before and nothing can be added or removed. Iblīs dwelt on the highest horizon, with thousands of acts of worship to his name, and gained nothing by them, because he was not worthy. Approval and wrath are beginningless attributes, so rolled-up sleeves and determined steps bring no profit on their own. One day ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb came upon Iblīs, seized him by the collar and told him he had been looking for him for a long time.

### In short

- Verses 6 and 7 describe the open disbelievers, and the thirteen verses after them describe the hypocrites. Together with the first five verses they divide mankind by its response to guidance, the only division that matters.
- Kufr means covering the truth. In the Sharīʿah it is denying anything that must be believed, even a single established teaching.
- Indhār is a warning born of compassion, which is why "warner" is a title reserved for the prophets.
- Warning and silence are the same for those who Allah knew would die in disbelief, like Abū Jahl and Abū Lahab, not for disbelievers in general, many of whom later believed. And it is never the same for the one who calls, who is rewarded for his effort whatever the result.

7.text:
The reason the warning changes nothing for them follows at once. "Allah has sealed their hearts and their hearing, and their sight is covered. They will suffer a tremendous punishment". A seal keeps anything from entering. A covering keeps anything from being seen. When the heart, the hearing and the sight are all shut, every path by which truth might reach a person is closed, and what remains is the punishment of the next world.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Allah has sealed their hearts and their hearing"** means He has stamped them. As-Suddī said that khatama means "He sealed". Qatādah said that Shayṭān gained control of them when they obeyed him, so Allah sealed their hearts, their ears and their eyes, leaving them unable to see guidance, to hear it, or to grasp and understand it. Ibn Jurayj reported Mujāhid's explanation: the seal is a stamp, and it comes about when sin settles in the heart and surrounds it from every side, so that the heart's drowning in sin becomes a stamp, that is, a seal. Ibn Jurayj added that the seal is set on both the heart and the hearing. The seal on the heart makes certain that no good enters it. The seal on the hearing is something deposited in the ears so that the person cannot profit from the truth he hears. Allah has locked their falsehood inside their hearts, and sealed their hearing so that they neither listen to the truth nor accept it. In as-Suddī's commentary, Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Masʿūd said it means that they neither understand nor hear.

**"and their sight is covered"** means a veil or shield lies over their eyes, and the truth in its clarity is hidden from them. In reciting, it is correct to pause after "their hearing" and then continue with "and their sight is covered", because the stamp belongs to the heart and the hearing while the covering, ghishāwah, belongs to the eyes. The distinction is deliberate. An idea can enter the heart from any direction, and a sound can enter the ears from any direction, so the only way to block them is to seal them. The eyes work in one direction only and see only what lies in front of them, so a covering is enough to stop them.

**"They will suffer a tremendous punishment"** means a dreadful torment in the Hereafter, intense and everlasting.

### Whom the verse was about

The verse is said to have been about particular Jews of Madinah: Ḥuyayy ibn Akhṭab, his kinsman Judayy ibn Akhṭab, and Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf. Another view names three of the Makkan idolaters instead: al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah and the two brothers ʿUtbah and Shaybah, sons of Rabīʿah.

### How a heart gets sealed

Mujāhid taught that the stain is less serious than the stamp, and the stamp less serious than the lock, which is the worst. Al-Aʿmash described Mujāhid showing it with his hand: the heart, they used to say, is like an open palm. When the servant commits a sin, part of it rolls up, and he closed his index finger. Another sin, and another part rolls up, and he closed another finger, until all his fingers were closed. Then, he said, the heart is sealed. Mujāhid said this is what the Qur'an calls the rān, the stain: "But no! In fact, their hearts have been stained by all ˹the evil˺ they used to commit" (83:14). Ibn Jarīr held that this stain is the truth of the matter.

A hadith reported from Abū Hurayrah says the same. When a man sins, a black dot appears on his heart. The first dot troubles him, the way a smudge on white cloth is always displeasing, but if instead of asking Allah's pardon he sins again, another dot appears, and with every new sin the dots multiply until the whole heart is dark, and then he can no longer see good as good or evil as evil, and loses the power to tell them apart. The Prophet ﷺ added that this darkness is what the Qur'an calls rayn, rust, and recited the verse above. This is recorded in Mishkāt from the Musnad of Aḥmad and from at-Tirmidhī. At-Tirmidhī, an-Nasāʾī and Ibn Mājah recorded the hadith, and at-Tirmidhī graded it ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ. In another sound hadith from Abū Hurayrah, recorded by at-Tirmidhī, the Prophet ﷺ said that when a man commits a sin his heart darkens, and if he seeks Allah's forgiveness it becomes clear again.

Ḥudhayfah's hadith, recorded in the Ṣaḥīḥ, describes the process on a larger scale. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that trials are presented to hearts one after another, like the straws woven into a reed mat. Any heart that absorbs a trial gets a black spot marked on it, and any heart that rejects it gets a white spot, until hearts fall into two kinds: one white like smooth rock, which no trial will harm as long as the heavens and the earth remain, and one black and dull like an overturned cup, which no longer recognises good or rejects evil.

### Punishment in this world as well as the next

These two verses show that the real punishment for disbelief, and for some sins, comes in the next world. But some punishment can come for certain sins in this world too, and sometimes it takes a very grave form: the divine favour that helps a person reform is withdrawn, so that he stops thinking about how his deeds will be judged on the Day of Judgment, grows in disobedience, and finally loses even the awareness of evil. Some of the early scholars put it this way: one punishment for a bad deed is another bad deed that follows it, and one reward for a good deed is another good deed that follows it. Allah's way with people who become so stubborn in denial that they will not hear the truth or weigh a clear argument is to give them this kind of punishment already in this world. Their hearts get sealed and their ears and eyes shut against the truth, so that, as far as truth is concerned, they are left with no mind for thinking, no eyes for seeing and no ears for hearing. The last phrase of the verse adds the grievous punishment kept for them in the next world.

### A doubt removed

A question is sometimes raised. If Allah Himself sealed their hearts and blocked their senses, are they not helpless, and how can they be blamed and punished for disbelief they did not choose? The answer lies in reading this verse together with the verse on rust, 83:14, which makes plain that it was their own arrogance and evil deeds that settled on their hearts as rust. It is that same rust which this verse calls a seal and a covering. By choosing arrogance and pride they wilfully destroyed their own capacity to accept the truth, and so they are the authors of their own ruin. Allah, as the Creator of all the actions of His creatures, attributes the sealing to Himself, and in doing so points out that when these people insisted, by their own choice, on wrecking their aptitude for truth, He produced in their hearts and senses the insensitivity that is His way in such cases. Al-Qurṭubī said that the ummah agrees on this: Allah describes Himself as the One who seals and closes the disbelievers' hearts, and does so to punish their disbelief, as in the verse about the People of the Book: "it is Allah Who has sealed their hearts for their disbelief, so they do not believe except for a few" (4:155). He also cited the Prophet's ﷺ supplication, "O Turner of hearts, make our hearts firm on Your religion."

Put in modern terms, the minds of people who do not take the call of truth seriously, who are proud and worldly, are wrapped in an invisible veil that makes them impervious to it. A person prejudiced against something cannot see its reasonableness even when the signs in its favour are clear.

### Two kinds of seal

On one heart the seal of estrangement was placed, and its owner stayed in disbelief. On another the seal of perplexity was placed, and its owner stayed in lethargy. The first is a stranger, driven off, the road lost. The second is helpless, stuck on the road, kept back from the Friend by something other than the Friend. Anything that holds you back from the road is a hindrance, whether it is called disbelief or faith, and any image that keeps you from the Friend is a hindrance, whether it is ugly or beautiful. Not everyone who escapes disbelief reaches the Real. He reaches that only when he escapes from himself. Escaping disbelief brings a person to familiarity, and escaping from himself brings him to friendship, and between familiarity and friendship lie a thousand stations, and between love and the Friend a thousand valleys.

### What comes next

Four verses at the start of the surah described the believers, and these two described the disbelievers, who are at fault inside and out. Next Allah describes the hypocrites, who look good on the outside but are not so within. Because hypocrisy is hard to see and many people do not grasp its reality, Allah describes it in detail, and each of the traits He lists is itself a kind of hypocrisy. Two whole surahs, Barāʾah (chapter 9) and al-Munāfiqūn (chapter 63), were revealed about the hypocrites, and they are mentioned in an-Nūr (chapter 24) and other surahs, so that people would know what they look like and steer clear of their ways and errors.

### In short

- The heart and the hearing are "sealed" because ideas and sounds come from every direction. The eyes are "covered" because they look one way only.
- The seal is not arbitrary. Sin stains the heart dot by dot, finger by finger, until it is dark all over. That is the rust of 83:14, and this verse calls the same rust a seal and a covering.
- Allah attributes the sealing to Himself as the Creator of all acts, but the disbelievers brought it on themselves by their arrogance, so they are answerable for it, and the ummah agrees that the seal is a punishment for disbelief.
- Losing the sense of right and wrong is itself a punishment in this life. The "tremendous punishment" waits in the next.

8.text:
A third group now enters. "And there are some who say, “We believe in Allah and the Last Day,” yet they are not ˹true˺ believers". The believers were described in four verses and the open disbelievers in two. The next thirteen verses describe the hypocrites, people whose tongues say one thing while their hearts hold another. Because hypocrisy is hard to see, the Qur'an takes its time over it, and this verse opens the portrait with the hypocrite's defining act: a claim of faith that is not true.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And there are some who say"** uses the Arabic man yaqūl, which is singular in form but plural in sense, and the verse goes on to speak of them with a plural pronoun, "they". The verses that follow were revealed about the hypocrites.

**"We believe in Allah and the Last Day"** is what they said openly, claiming to be genuine in it. The Last Day is the Day of Resurrection, so called because it is the very last day. They professed belief in rising after death and in being repaid for their deeds.

**"yet they are not ˹true˺ believers"** means they did not believe in secret and were not genuine. They uttered the words with their tongues only. The same is said of them elsewhere: "When the hypocrites come to you ˹O Prophet˺, they say, “We bear witness that you are certainly the Messenger of Allah”—and surely Allah knows that you are His Messenger—but Allah bears witness that the hypocrites are truly liars" (63:1). They said such things only when they met the believers, not because they believed them, and they stressed their faith in Allah and the Last Day with their words when the reality was otherwise. So Allah declared that they lie in their very testimony of faith.

### What hypocrisy is

Nifāq means to show agreement on the outside and to hide evil within. It is of more than one kind. There is hypocrisy in belief, which keeps its people in Hell forever, and there is hypocrisy in conduct, which is among the major sins. Ibn Jurayj described the hypocrite: what he actually does differs from what he announces, what he hides differs from what he says, and the way he comes in and sits among people is not the way he goes out and behaves in their absence.

Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq reported Ibn ʿAbbās's explanation that the verse refers to the hypocrites among the Aws and the Khazraj and to those who behaved as they did. Abū al-ʿĀliyah, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah and as-Suddī explained it the same way. Allah revealed the traits of the hypocrites so that the believers would not be fooled by their outward appearance and would be spared a great harm. Otherwise the believers might have taken them for believers when they were in fact disbelievers, and to count sinners among the righteous is extremely dangerous.

### How hypocrisy began

The verses on the hypocrites were revealed in Madinah, because there were no hypocrites in Makkah. The situation there was the reverse: some people were forced to pretend disbelief while their hearts held faith. Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ migrated to Madinah, where the Anṣār of the Aws and the Khazraj lived. They had worshipped idols in the days of ignorance like the other Arabs. Three Jewish tribes lived there too: Banū Qaynuqāʿ, allies of the Khazraj, and Banū an-Naḍīr and Banū Qurayẓah, allies of the Aws. Many of the Aws and Khazraj embraced Islam, but only a few of the Jews did, among them ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām. In the early period there were still no hypocrites, because the Muslims were not yet strong enough to be feared. On the contrary, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ made peace treaties with the Jews and with several Arab tribes around the city. Then the battle of Badr took place and Allah gave Islam and its people the victory. ʿAbdullāh ibn Ubayy ibn Salūl was a leading man of Madinah, chief of the Khazraj, and in the days of ignorance he had been the master of both tribes. The people were about to crown him king when the message reached Madinah and many embraced Islam, and his heart filled with hatred for Islam and its people. When Badr was fought he said that Allah's religion had now become established, so he pretended to be a Muslim, and so did many like him, and many from among the People of the Book. That is when hypocrisy began, in Madinah and among the nomad tribes around it. There were no hypocrites among the Emigrants, because they had emigrated of their own free will, seeking Allah's pleasure. A Muslim who emigrated from Makkah had to leave behind all his wealth, his children and his land, and he did it for Allah's reward in the Hereafter.

### Even they avoided an outright lie

The wording of their claim shows how ugly lying is. Even the hypocrites, with all their hostility to Islam, tried as far as possible to avoid it. When they claimed to be Muslims they mentioned only their faith in Allah and in the Day of Judgment and left out faith in the Prophet ﷺ, for fear of stating a plain lie.

### The mind of a hypocrite

People who put worldly interests and expediency first find total, unconditional devotion to truth unwise, because their real loyalty is to their interests, and they can attach themselves to the truth only on the surface. They think themselves clever: safe in this world, and at the same time counted among the pious. It is wishful thinking, a product of imagination rather than a fact of life.

### Why Allah let there be hypocrites

The inner reading traces the hypocrites' hypocrisy back to the eminence of the Prophet ﷺ, in two ways, one of jealousy and one of mercy. He was the beloved of the Real, and his beauty and perfection passed beyond what understanding and imagination can hold, so Allah, out of jealousy, kept him veiled behind His protection and used the hypocrisy of the hypocrites as a mask over that beauty. He was veiled from the people of the world so that no one recognised him as he really was: "you ˹O Prophet˺ may see them facing towards you, but they cannot see" (7:198). Had their hypocrisy not covered that shining face, all creatures would have cast dust over the unseen light. A sun so bright, a light so brilliant, needed a hypocrisy of the kind ʿAbdullāh ibn Ubayy ibn Salūl and his sort supplied. Without it, that radiant beauty would have affected the children of Ādam more than the beauty of ʿĪsā (Jesus) affected his people, who said, "The Messiah is the son of Allah" (9:30). A simile is given. The disk of the sun, whose rays shine from the fourth heaven, has its face turned toward the fifth. Allah created angels and entrusted the disk to them, and created deserts full of snow before them, from which they lift mountain after mountain of snow and dash it against the sun's disk to break its heat, since otherwise the world would burn from its shine and heat. In the same way the hypocrites' hypocrisy was thrown against the presence of that sun of good fortune, or else all the creatures would have tied on the belt of associating partners with Allah. And the mercy: that paragon of the world was all gentleness, as he said of himself, "I am a guided mercy", and as Allah said, "We have sent you ˹O Prophet˺ only as a mercy for the whole world" (21:107).

### In short

- Nifāq is agreement on the outside with evil hidden inside. In belief it is eternal ruin, in conduct a major sin.
- The hypocrites professed Allah and the Last Day only with their tongues, and Allah exposed their traits so that the believers would not be taken in.
- There were no hypocrites in Makkah and none among the Emigrants. Hypocrisy began in Madinah after Badr, led by ʿAbdullāh ibn Ubayy ibn Salūl, when Islam became too strong to oppose openly.
- Even the hypocrites avoided stating a bare lie about the Prophet ﷺ, which shows how contemptible lying is.

9.text:
The next verse says what the false profession was for. "They seek to deceive Allah and the believers, yet they only deceive themselves, but they fail to perceive it". They thought their words bought them safety and standing. In fact the whole scheme turned back on them, and they could not see it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"They seek to deceive Allah and the believers"** means they show faith outwardly while hiding disbelief, so as to escape the rulings that would apply to them in this world. Secretly they went against Allah and denied Him. It is also said that they were so bold with Allah that they thought they had actually deceived Him. They imagined that this behaviour would mislead Allah, or that the words they uttered would count for them with Him, which shows how total their ignorance was. They expected to fool Allah the way they might fool some of the believers, and on the Day of Judgment they will try the same thing: "they will ˹falsely˺ swear to Him as they swear to you, thinking they have something to stand on. Indeed, it is they who are the ˹total˺ liars" (58:18). The believers they tried to deceive were Abū Bakr and all the Companions of Muhammad ﷺ. The mention of Allah here, when the practical target was the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims, carries a lesson. Probably none of them intended to deceive Allah or even imagined it possible. What they were doing was trying to deceive His Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims, and Allah equated that with an attempt to deceive Him. Whoever is insolent toward a prophet or a man of Allah is in the end insolent toward Allah Himself, and above all when it is the Prophet ﷺ, who stands at the head of all created beings. Some also read the mention of Allah in this verse as there for rhetorical force.

**"yet they only deceive themselves"** because the evil consequences of their deception rebound on them. They are disgraced in this world when Allah informs His Prophet ﷺ of what they hide, and they are punished in the Hereafter. Allah refuted their scheme: "Surely the hypocrites seek to deceive Allah, but He outwits them" (4:142). Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded Ibn Jurayj's comment on that verse: the hypocrites pronounce the testimony that there is no god but Allah in order to make their blood and property inviolable, while hiding disbelief. The verb used, yukhādiʿūn, is the form that normally denotes a mutual action, though here it denotes a one-way act, as when someone says ʿāqabtu al-liṣṣa, "I punished the thief", using the same form. A variant reading has wa-mā yakhdaʿūn.

**"but they fail to perceive it"** means they do not realise that they are deceiving themselves, and they do not know that Allah informs His Prophet ﷺ of what lies hidden in their hearts. Allah knows all that is secret and has told the believers what these people are like.

### A portrait of the hypocrite

Saʿīd reported Qatādah's description. The hypocrite is slippery. His tongue speaks the truth while his heart and his deeds fight against it. He wakes up in one condition and goes to sleep in another, and goes to sleep in one and wakes up in another. He changes his mind like a ship that swings about whichever way the wind blows.

### The inner reading

The harm of their deception and its punishment come back to them, so it is as if they really did deceive themselves, since they cheapened and belittled themselves. No one suffered from what they did but themselves. They cut their own lifeblood. When someone knows the true nature of things, whoever sets out to deceive him deceives only himself. The allusion in the verse is to the person who has forgotten Allah's prior kindness, who says "mine, through me, from me, and I" when he should say "Yours, through You, from You, and You". That delusion is the hardest punishment of all. He sees a mirage, sarāb, and thinks it is drink, sharāb, "but when they approach it, they find it to be nothing. Instead, they find Allah there ˹in the Hereafter, ready˺ to settle their account" (24:39).

### In short

- The hypocrites hid disbelief behind a show of faith to secure their lives and property under Muslim rule, and imagined this would work even with Allah.
- Deceiving the Prophet ﷺ and the believers is treated by Allah as an attempt to deceive Him, a warning about how insolence toward His messengers is judged.
- Every such scheme rebounds: exposure in this world, since Allah tells His Prophet ﷺ what they hide, and punishment in the next. They alone are the losers, and they do not sense it.

10.text:
Why do they behave this way, and why can they not see the folly of it? "There is sickness in their hearts, and Allah ˹only˺ lets their sickness increase. They will suffer a painful punishment for their lies". The verse names a disease, states that it is getting worse, and then ties the punishment to one habit in particular: lying.

### Phrase by phrase

**"There is sickness in their hearts"** means doubt. That is how Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Masʿūd explained it, as reported through as-Suddī from Abū Mālik, Abū Ṣāliḥ and Murrah al-Hamdānī, along with other Companions, and Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas and Qatādah said the same. ʿAbdur-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said it is a disease in religion, not a bodily disease: they are the hypocrites, and the disease is the doubt they brought into Islam. Others gloss it as doubt, hypocrisy, conflict and darkness, a sickness that weakens the heart. The inner reading calls it the sickness of shirk.

**"and Allah ˹only˺ lets their sickness increase"** means He increases their doubt, or increases them in shameful conduct, as ʿAbdur-Raḥmān ibn Zayd put it, citing the verse about the hypocrites and each new surah: "as for those with sickness in their hearts, it has increased them only in wickedness upon their wickedness, and they die as disbelievers" (9:124-125), that is, evil added to their evil and deviation to their deviation. This is correct, and it is a punishment matched to the sin, as the early scholars said. The opposite is also true: "As for those who are ˹rightly˺ guided, He increases them in guidance and blesses them with righteousness" (47:17). The increase comes through what Allah reveals in the Qur'an, since they disbelieve each new revelation. Their doubt gains hesitation on top of uncertainty. They reap what they sowed, and in the inner reading they grow sicker as they imagine that they have saved themselves by deceiving the Muslims.

**"They will suffer a painful punishment for their lies"** means a painful torment in the Hereafter that reaches into their very hearts, in the lowest reaches of Hell, the price of lying against Allah and against people and of rejecting what Muhammad ﷺ brought. The hypocrites have two marks: they lie, and they deny the unseen. The word for their lying can be read yukadhdhibūn, that they called the Prophet of Allah ﷺ a liar, or yakdhibūn, that they lied when they said "we believe". The verse points in particular to ʿAbdullāh ibn Ubayy, Jadd ibn Qays and Muʿattib ibn Qushayr.

### Disease of the heart

In medicine, disease is a state in which the balance of elements that keep a person healthy is lost, so the body stops working properly and may be destroyed. In the language of the Qur'an and the hadith the word is also used of mental and spiritual states that keep a person from any degree of spiritual perfection, gradually stripping him of the ability to do good and even of ordinary human decency until he reaches spiritual death. Junayd of Baghdad said that bodily diseases come from the four humours falling out of balance, and diseases of the heart come from giving in to physical desires. The disease hidden in the hypocrites' hearts was disbelief and rejection of the truth, and it was as much a physical sickness as a spiritual one. Ingratitude to one's Creator and Sustainer and defiance of His commands is spiritual sickness, plainly. Hiding that disbelief for petty worldly gain, lacking the courage to speak one's mind, is another disease of the soul. And hypocrisy is a physical disease too, because the hypocrite is forever shuddering at the thought of exposure. Envy is a necessary ingredient of hypocrisy, so he cannot bear to see the Muslims grow stronger, and yet he cannot even relieve his heart of its venom. All that tension naturally comes out in bodily illness. Hypocrisy is a cancer that keeps growing. Every test in life pushes such people further from true religion and closer to their own world-centred "religion".

### The curse of lying

There is a subtle point in the last clause. The hypocrites' worst crime was their disbelief and their hypocrisy in faith itself, and they had other crimes besides, nursing envy and malice against the Muslims and actually conspiring against them. Yet the painful punishment is tied to their habit of lying. This hints that lying was at bottom their real crime, the one that led them step by step into hypocrisy and disbelief. Hypocrisy and disbelief are far greater crimes, but they grew out of the habit of lying. That is why the Qur'an puts lying beside idol worship in a single breath: "So shun the impurity of idolatry, and shun words of falsehood" (22:30).

### Did the Prophet ﷺ know who they were?

Those who say the Prophet ﷺ knew the hypocrites of his time have as their only evidence the hadith of Ḥudhayfah ibn al-Yamān, in which the Prophet ﷺ gave him the names of fourteen hypocrites during the expedition to Tabūk. They had plotted to kill him at night on a hill there by startling his camel so that she would throw him down the slope. Allah informed him of the plot, and he told Ḥudhayfah their names. About the rest, Allah said: "Some of the nomads around you ˹believers˺ are hypocrites, as are some of the people of Medina. They have mastered hypocrisy. They are not known to you ˹O Prophet˺; they are known to Us" (9:101), and "If the hypocrites, and those with sickness in their hearts, and rumour-mongers in Medina do not desist, We will certainly incite you ˹O Prophet˺ against them" (33:60-61). These verses prove that he was not told the identity of every hypocrite. He was told their traits, and he suspected certain people of having them: "Had We willed, We could have truly shown them to you ˹O Prophet˺, and you would have certainly recognized them by their appearance. But you will surely recognize them by their tone of speech" (47:30).

The most notorious hypocrite of the time was ʿAbdullāh ibn Ubayy ibn Salūl, and the Companion Zayd ibn Arqam gave truthful testimony to that effect. When ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb once raised the matter of Ibn Salūl with the Prophet ﷺ, he answered that he would not have the Arabs saying to one another that Muhammad kills his Companions. Yet when Ibn Salūl died the Prophet ﷺ prayed the funeral prayer over him and attended his burial as he did for other Muslims. It is recorded in the Ṣaḥīḥ that he said, "I was given the choice, and I chose," and in another narration, "If I knew that asking forgiveness for him more than seventy times would bring him forgiveness, I would do it."

### The half-hearted seeker

The inner reading applies the verse to anyone who has confused his ultimate aim with his worldly share and mixed his spiritual desire, irādah, with his whim, taking one step forward in desire for Allah and one step back toward the world and the lower self. He is neither a sincere seeker, a murīd, nor wholly heedless. Had the hypocrites been sincere in belief they would have been as safe from punishment in the Hereafter as they were in this world from the jizyah and the like, which polytheists and protected non-Muslims paid. Likewise, had the seeker been sincere in his desire, his heart would have reached toward the realities of communion, sincerity's blessings would have come to him, and he would have gained what he sought. Instead his state is the one in the saying: we were not firm, so justice will be firm with us and will not bend, and had we been sincere we would have been saved from trial. A barrier stands between the person whose worship has weakened and the degrees of the Gardens, and a barrier between the person whose spiritual desire has weakened and the intimate confidences of nearness. For those who lean on this world and follow their whims, reliance on the abode of illusion is itself a disease of the heart, and the disease grows as their greed grows. The more they get of the world, the more they crave what they have not got, and that hastens their punishment. Among the punishments that arrive at once are the scattering of their aims and the loss of all pleasure in life. These keep them from their Protector, and there is no enjoyment or rest for them in what they preferred when they followed their whims.

### In short

- The sickness is doubt, hypocrisy and the darkness that comes with them, a disease of religion rather than of the body, though hypocrisy's tension sickens the body too.
- Allah increases it as a punishment matched to the sin: each new revelation they reject deepens their doubt, just as each one deepens the believers' faith.
- The punishment is tied to lying because lying was the root habit from which their hypocrisy and disbelief grew. The Qur'an ranks falsehood beside idolatry.
- The Prophet ﷺ was told the hypocrites' traits, and fourteen names at Tabūk, but not the identity of every hypocrite. He still prayed over Ibn Salūl, the worst of them, out of hope for his forgiveness.

11.text:
The hypocrites did not see themselves as wreckers. "When they are told, “Do not spread corruption in the land,” they reply, “We are only peace-makers!”". Their activities threatened general disorder, yet they presented themselves as men of goodwill who were serving peace and order. This verse records the claim, and the next refutes it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"When they are told"** means when the believers, or the Prophet ﷺ, say this to them. One reading takes the people addressed to be the Jews, warned against turning people away from the religion of Muhammad ﷺ.

**"Do not spread corruption in the land"** means, according to Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Masʿūd in as-Suddī's commentary, do not commit disbelief and acts of disobedience. Abū al-ʿĀliyah, as reported by Abū Jaʿfar from ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, said it means do not disobey Allah on the earth, because the hypocrites' corruption is disobedience to Allah. Whoever disobeys Allah on the earth, or orders that He be disobeyed, has spread corruption on it, and peace in the earth and in the heavens is secured by obedience. Ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas and Qatādah said the same. The corruption includes disbelief, hindering people from faith, and ruining things through rejection of the truth and disobedience.

**"We are only peace-makers!"** The Arabic innamā, "only", conveys not just emphasis but exclusivity: they claimed to be nothing but reformers, servants of order, whose activities could have nothing to do with disorder. They meant that they were not engaging in corruption at all, and that they were putting things right through obedience. In practice they meant something more specific. They wanted friendship with both sides, believers and disbelievers alike, and peace with each. Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq reported Ibn ʿAbbās's explanation: they claimed to be making amends between the believers and the People of the Book.

### How the hypocrites corrupt the land

Ibn Jarīr spelled out their corruption. They disobey their Lord on His earth and persist in what He forbade. They abandon what He made obligatory and doubt His religion, although He accepts no deed from anyone without faith in His religion and certainty of its truth. They lie to the believers, saying the opposite of the doubt and hesitation in their hearts. They help, as far as they are able, those who work against Allah's loyal friends, and they back the deniers of Allah, of His Books and of His Messengers. That is how the hypocrites corrupt the earth while thinking they are doing good on it. This is right, and taking the disbelievers as allies is itself one of the kinds of corruption in the land. Allah said, "As for the disbelievers, they are guardians of one another. And unless you ˹believers˺ act likewise, there will be great oppression and corruption in the land" (8:73), so cutting the bond of loyalty between believers and disbelievers, and "O believers! Do not take disbelievers as allies instead of the believers. Would you like to give Allah solid proof against yourselves" (4:144), followed by "Surely the hypocrites will be in the lowest depths of the Fire" (4:145). Because the hypocrite looks like a believer on the outside, he confuses the true believers. His deceit is corruption twice over: he deceives the believers by professing what he does not believe, and he backs the disbelievers against them.

### Claims do not decide the question

Words alone do not settle whether someone is working for order or disorder. What thief calls himself a thief? The test is what a person does, not what he says. If his activities produce mischief he is a mischief-maker even if he never intended it. Among the things that spread disorder, some are recognised by everyone as corruption, such as theft, robbery, murder and rape, and every sensible, conscientious person keeps away from them. Others do not look like corruption on the outside but work unseen, destroying people's morals, which in turn opens the door to every kind of disorder. That is exactly what the hypocrites were doing. They did keep away from theft and robbery, and on that basis they denied being corrupters and insisted that they served order. But all the while their malice and envy had free rein as they plotted with the Muslims' enemies, and these are the things that finally bring a man down to the level of beasts. They called their own policy reform and prized it because it let them steer a safe course without clashing with anyone, which only shows how twisted their reasoning was.

### The seeker who turns back

In the inner reading the verse alludes to what happens when thoughts of warning come quietly to a heart, calling it to right conduct, and the person answers with self-indulgent interpretations, deceiving himself about what in fact testifies to the hardness of his heart. When the Real's proof came to them in those visiting thoughts and they denied it, Allah took the blessing out of their states and gave them in exchange an ear deaf to Him. Their affliction lies in resisting the path and losing faith in it. Just as an apostate is a fiercer enemy to the Muslims than others, so the one who turns back from spiritual desire to the world and ordinary habits is the worst of people in rejecting this path and the furthest from its followers. As the proverb says, whoever loses his stored grain to fire wishes the same on others. The sincere people of the path held that no help should be taken from those who have deserted the way, on the pattern of the Messenger ﷺ, who refused the zakāt of Thaʿlabah.

### In short

- Corruption in the land, in the Companions' explanation, is disbelief and disobedience, and peace on earth is secured by obedience to Allah.
- The hypocrites' particular corruption was doubting the religion, lying to the believers, and quietly allying with the disbelievers against them while posing as peacemakers between the two sides.
- "Only" in their reply claims exclusivity: nothing but reformers. But it is deeds, not claims, that make a reformer or a corrupter.
- Hidden moral corruption is worse than open crime because it destroys the people on whom all order depends.

12.text:
Allah answers their claim directly. "Indeed, it is they who are the corruptors, but they fail to perceive it". The verse opens with an alerting particle meant to make the hearer sit up. The people who called themselves the servants of peace are the very agents of disorder, and the second half of the verse adds something worse: they do not even know it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Indeed"** translates a-lā, a word used to alert the listener and give emphasis to what follows. Allah, exalted is He, refutes them with it.

**"it is they who are the corruptors"** means that the hypocrites' behaviour, and their claim that it was all for peace, was itself corruption. Their hindering of others from the religion was corruption. Their actions were the cause of the ruin they denied.

**"but they fail to perceive it"** means that in their ignorance they did not see it as corruption. It is also said that it means the followers do not know that their leaders are misleading them. Two things follow from Allah's comment. First, the hypocrites' activities really did produce disorder in the land. Second, they did not engage in them with the express intention of creating disorder. They were not even aware that their actions could cause it.

### Why the hidden corrupter is more dangerous

Once a person has lost his feeling for ethical values and ordinary decency, even an average man turns into an agent of social disorder, and of a disorder far greater than thieves, robbers or even wild beasts can produce. Robbers and beasts can be held in check by the physical force of law and government. But men make the laws and men enforce them, and what becomes of law when man stops being man is on view across the world today. It is assumed on every side that humanity is marching forward and that modern man is civilisation's summit. Educational institutions cover every hamlet on earth, legislatures buzz night and day, bodies for enforcing the law spend billions, and bureaucratic offices multiply. Yet crime and disorder keep step with the march of civilisation. The reason is simple. Law is not an automatic machine. It needs men to make it work, and when man ceases to be man, neither laws nor bureaucratic agencies can cure the all-pervading disorder. That is why the greatest benefactor of mankind, the Prophet ﷺ, put all his attention into making men real men, in the fullest sense of the word. Once that is achieved, crime and disorder end by themselves, without huge police forces and vast systems of courts. As long as people in certain parts of the world acted on his teachings, they saw a peace and order never witnessed before, and not likely to be seen again where his teachings are dropped or ignored.

In practical terms the core of his teaching is fear of Allah and concern for the assessment of one's deeds on the Day of Judgment. Where these are missing, no constitution or legal code, no administrative body or university can force or persuade a person to keep away from crime. Those who run the world today keep inventing new administrative measures against crime while neglecting the very soul of administration, the fear of Allah, and even deploying the means of destroying it, with the necessary result that the remedy feeds the disease.

### Reformers in name

Thieves, robbers and everyone who makes trouble in the open are easy enough to deal with. The troublemakers described in these verses always appear dressed as reformers, waving colourful schemes of social improvement that are a mask for private interests, and raising the slogan, "We are only peace-makers!" That is why Allah, having told people not to spread corruption on the earth, also said elsewhere, "And Allah knows who intends harm and who intends good" (2:220). Only Allah knows what is in people's hearts and what they intend, and only He knows the real nature of each human act and where it leads, whether it serves order or disorder. So to serve the cause of order it is not enough to intend it. Far more essential is to bring one's thinking and action into line with the Sharīʿah, because an action, however well meant, can end in mischief and disorder if the Sharīʿah does not guide it. If such people thought deeply they would realise that reform on earth can come only from man's giving himself up to Allah alone, and that obstructing any movement meant to strengthen man's bond with his Lord's will is creating disorder on earth. Their seemingly profitable business runs at a loss, because they trade pure truth for an adulterated version that benefits no one.

### A smaller evil, and a way out

If the hypocrite had stayed an open disbeliever instead of pretending to be a Muslim, the harm from him would have been less. Better still, if he became sincere with Allah and made his deeds match his words, he would succeed.

### The inner reading

It is said that exposing liars needs nothing more than saying to their face, "You have lied." When they said, "We are only peace-makers!", the Real showed them to be liars: "Indeed, it is they who are the corruptors, but they fail to perceive it," meaning, We are aware of them and have exposed them.

### In short

- The emphatic opening turns their claim on its head: the self-styled peacemakers are the corrupters, and they really did spread disorder.
- They did not perceive it, either because they had no intention of corruption or because followers could not see where their leaders were taking them.
- Law cannot replace conscience. The Prophet ﷺ cured disorder by making men whole, through fear of Allah and mindfulness of the Judgment.
- Good intentions do not make a reformer. Only action guided by the Sharīʿah does, and Allah alone knows who intends harm and who intends good.

13.text:
The hypocrites were also offered a measure of true faith and sneered at it. "And when they are told, “Believe as others believe,” they reply, “Will we believe as the fools believe?” Indeed, it is they who are fools, but they do not know". The "others" are the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ. The hypocrites looked down on them as simpletons, and Allah returned the word to its rightful owners.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And when they are told, “Believe as others believe,”"** means: believe the way the believers do, in Allah and His angels, in His Books and His Messengers, in the Resurrection, in Paradise and in Hell, and obey Allah and His Messenger by keeping His commands and avoiding His prohibitions. The Arabic word for "others" is an-nās, the people, and by agreement of the scholars it refers here to the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ, because they were the people who had embraced faith and accepted the Qur'an as the word of Allah while it was being revealed. One reading addresses the verse to the Jews, telling them to believe in Muhammad ﷺ as ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām and his companions had.

**"they reply, “Will we believe as the fools believe?”"** By "the fools", may Allah curse the hypocrites, they meant the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. That is the explanation of Abū al-ʿĀliyah, of as-Suddī with a chain to Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd and other Companions, and of ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas and ʿAbdur-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam. Their meaning was: are we to be of the same rank as them, on the same road, when they are fools? Should we believe in Muhammad ﷺ and the Qur'an as the stupid and ignorant do? No, we will not follow their way. They spoke looking down on people and mocking them. A fool, safīh, is the ignorant, simple-minded person with little knowledge of what benefits and what harms. That is why, according to most scholars, the word covers children in the verse, "Do not entrust the incapable ˹among your dependants˺ with your wealth which Allah has made a means of support for you" (4:5).

**"Indeed, it is they who are fools, but they do not know"** is Allah's answer. He affirms that the hypocrites themselves are the fools, the stupid and ignorant ones, and adds that they do not know it. Being so thoroughly ignorant, they are unaware of their own deviation and ignorance, and that is more dangerous, a worse blindness, and further from the truth than the state of someone who knows.

### The Companions as the measure of faith

The verse sets a criterion of true faith before the hypocrites: believe as the people have believed. It shows that the only faith acceptable to Allah is faith like that of the Companions, and that anyone else's faith deserves the name only when he believes in the same things in the same way they did. Their faith is the touchstone for testing the faith of all other Muslims. Any belief or practice that departs from their faith and practice, however attractive it looks or however good the intention behind it, is invalid in the Sharīʿah. Scholars are agreed on this position. It is also worth noticing that the hypocrites called the Companions fools. Those who go astray have always been like this: whoever tries to show them the right road is, in their eyes, ignorant and stupid. But who, the Qur'an asks, is more stupid than the man who refuses to see clear signs? To people whose loyalty is to worldly interest, the believers who act purely for the truth seem to be ruining themselves for nothing.

The verse after this one shows the hypocrites' two faces. Among the Muslims they declared their faith loudly, and back among their own people they gave assurances that their ancestors' way had never been abandoned and that they sat with the Muslims only to mock them.

### Does the category of hypocrite still exist?

It has been debated whether the distinction between kufr and nifāq still applies after the Prophet's ﷺ time. The correct position is this. While he lived, a hypocrite could be identified and declared one in two ways. Either Allah informed the Prophet ﷺ by revelation that a particular man was not a Muslim at heart, or the man exposed himself by a word or deed openly repugnant to the Islamic creed or practice, so providing clear evidence against himself. Revelation ended when the Prophet ﷺ left this world, so the first way is no longer available. The second remains. If a person is found, on evidence, guilty in word or deed of rejecting, opposing, distorting or scorning the basic doctrines of Islam established beyond denial by the Qur'an, the hadith and ijmāʿ, consensus, he is regarded as a munāfiq despite his claim to be a true Muslim. The Qur'an gives such a person the name mulḥid, heretic, as in "those who abuse Our revelations" (41:40), and the hadith calls him a zindīq. Since his kufr is proved by clear and definite evidence, the Sharīʿah does not place him in a separate category but treats him as it treats any other kāfir. That is why the authoritative scholars agree that after the Prophet ﷺ the question of hypocrites ceased to be a live one: anyone who is not a genuine Muslim is counted a kāfir. Al-ʿAynī, commenting on al-Bukhārī, relates from Imām Mālik that since the Prophet's ﷺ days this is the one remaining mark of hypocrisy, and that a man who carries it may be called a hypocrite.

### Worthy and unworthy

The inner reading turns the verse into praise of the Lord: generous, renowned, wise in what He enacts, true in promise, pure in justice, complete in bounty and eternal in love, who shows what He wants and adorns as He wants. Each person has a name, and in each heart lies His mark. On some is the stamp of worthiness and on others the brand of unworthiness. The worthy are brought along the road of bounty, mounted on approval, escorted by gentleness, at the hour of generous giving, at the turning toward nearness. The unworthy are driven into the street of justice, mounted on wrath, escorted by abandonment, at the turning toward deprivation. Neither that nearness nor this deprivation came from water or clay, since on the day the two were written out there was neither water nor clay, only beginningless bounty and gentleness and everlasting severity and justice. The first was the portion of those who purify themselves and the second the portion of the hypocrites. The master of the path lamented the apportioning that went before him and the words spoken by the One who sees Himself, asking what good it does him to be happy or distraught when what frightens him is what the Powerful decreed in the Beginningless. The hypocrites had fallen under justice's garment, yet they approved of themselves and believed their name was good, and called the purifiers, the truthful and the Messenger's Companions "fools". The Lord of the Worlds, in His generosity, answered on their behalf: the fools are not those men but the ones who call them fools. When someone no longer belongs to himself, Allah belongs to him. When someone tightens his belt to obey Allah's commands, Allah joins him. The disbelievers told the Prophet ﷺ he was possessed, "O you to whom the Reminder is revealed! You must be insane!" (15:6), and Allah answered, "By the grace of your Lord, you ˹O Prophet˺ are not insane" (68:2). You are My friend, approved by Me. What harm is it to you if they do not approve of you? What you need is My approval. A friend must be approved by the Friend, not by the city.

### In short

- "Others" means the Companions, by consensus, and their faith is the standard by which every later Muslim's faith is measured. Whatever departs from it is invalid, however good it looks.
- The hypocrites called the Companions fools. Allah ruled that the hypocrites are the fools, and not knowing it makes their state worse.
- After the Prophet ﷺ there is no revelation to unmask hypocrites. Anyone exposed by his own words or deeds as denying the established basics of Islam is simply a kāfir, whatever he calls himself.
- Those who mock the believers are answered by Allah Himself, as He answered those who called His Prophet ﷺ mad.

14.text:
Now the hypocrites are shown with both faces at once. "When they meet the believers they say, “We believe.” But when alone with their evil associates they say, “We are definitely with you; we were only mocking.”" In the company of the Muslims they loudly professed Islam. Back among their own leaders they explained that the profession was a joke at the believers' expense. The verse quotes them in both settings, and the next verse answers.

### Phrase by phrase

**"When they meet the believers"** means when they fall in with Abū Bakr and his companions. The Arabic laqū is originally laquyū, with the ḍammah dropped as too heavy to pronounce and the unvowelled yāʾ dropped before the wāw.

**"they say, “We believe.”"** They claimed to believe deep in their hearts and to be as genuine in their faith as the believers were in theirs. They did it to misdirect, mislead and deceive the believers, to pose as loyal friends, and because they expected it to pay: they wanted a share of whatever gains and benefits the believers might come by.

**"But when alone with their evil associates"** means when they went off by themselves and returned to their devils, that is, their leaders and masters among the Jewish rabbis, the hypocrites and the idolaters. Ibn Jarīr said that the devils of every kind of creature are the mischief-makers among them, and that there are human devils as well as jinn devils, as Allah said: "And so We have made for every prophet enemies—devilish humans and jinn—whispering to one another with elegant words of deception" (6:112). One report names five such leaders: Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf in Madinah, Abū Burdah al-Aslamī among Banū Aslam, Ibn as-Sawdāʾ in ash-Shām, ʿAbd ad-Dār in Juhaynah and ʿAwf ibn ʿĀmir among Banū ʿĀmir.

**"they say, “We are definitely with you"** means: we are with you in religion, we follow your religion in secret.

**"we were only mocking.”"** Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq reported Ibn ʿAbbās's explanation: we are with you, and we were only mocking those people and deceiving them. Through aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, Ibn ʿAbbās said it means they were mocking the Companions of Muhammad ﷺ, and ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas and Qatādah said the same. They were mocking the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions by feigning belief.

### The occasion of revelation

Through Abū Ṣāliḥ, Ibn ʿAbbās said that the verse was revealed about ʿAbdullāh ibn Ubayy and his followers. They went out one day and were met by a group of the Prophet's ﷺ Companions. ʿAbdullāh ibn Ubayy said to his people, "Watch how I keep these fools off you." He went forward and took the hand of Abū Bakr aṣ-Ṣiddīq, and said: welcome to the truthful one, chief of Banū Tamīm, leader of Islam, the Messenger's companion in the cave, who spent himself and his wealth for him. Then he took the hand of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb: welcome to the chief of Banū ʿAdī ibn Kaʿb, the one who separates truth from falsehood, firm in Allah's religion, who likewise spent himself and his wealth for the Messenger. Then he took the hand of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib: welcome to the Messenger's cousin and his son-in-law, chief of Banū Hāshim after the Messenger himself. Then the two groups parted. ʿAbdullāh asked his companions, "How did I do? When you meet them, do as I did," and they praised him. When the Muslims returned to the Prophet ﷺ and told him what had happened, Allah sent down this verse.

### Where the verse stands

The surah opened by declaring the Qur'an beyond doubt, and its first twenty verses draw the features of those who believe in it and those who do not. The first five deal with the believers under the title of the mindful, the next two with the disbelievers who were open and violent in their hostility, and the following thirteen with the crafty disbelievers who claimed to be Muslims but were not, whom the Qur'an calls the hypocrites. The first two of these thirteen verses, 8 and 9, define the hypocrites' behaviour, exposing their claim to be Muslims as false and deceitful, an attempt to be clever. No one can deceive Allah, and probably they never imagined they could, but the Qur'an in a sense equates trying to deceive the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims with trying to deceive Allah Himself. Such an attempt has only one result: they deceive no one but themselves, because Allah cannot be deceived and revelation protects His Prophet ﷺ from every trick, so that the hypocrites themselves bear the punishment for their presumption in both worlds. As for Allah making them grow in their sickness, they were jealous of the Muslims' growing strength, and it was Allah's will to make the Muslims stronger still, as the hypocrites could see for themselves, which fed their bile and kept the disease of their hearts growing. Verses 11 and 12 describe their insensibility and ignorance: they counted their defects as merits. Verse 13 shows the other side of that corruption: the merit of others, the pure faith of the Muslims, turned in their eyes into a defect, even into something contemptible. When they openly refused to believe as others believed and called the Muslims fools, they could have been so outspoken only in front of the poorer Muslims, since otherwise they were very careful to keep their disbelief hidden. The present verse shows their two-facedness and trickery.

### What faith really is

Reflection on these verses reveals the true nature of Islam and faith, and of disbelief. The Qur'an reports the hypocrites' claim, "We believe in Allah" (2:8), and refutes it at once: they are not believers. To grasp the point fully, keep in mind that the hypocrites in question were Jews. Belief in Allah and the Hereafter was an essential part of their creed too. What their creed, as their scholars defined it, did not include was belief in the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ. So when they professed Islam they very cleverly left out faith in the Prophet ﷺ and named only belief in Allah and belief in the Hereafter. As far as those words go they could not be called liars, yet the Qur'an rejects their claim to be Muslims and calls them liars. Why?

Because to be a Muslim it is not enough to profess faith in Allah and the Hereafter in whatever form suits one's individual or collective fancy. Idolaters of every kind believe in Allah in some fashion and hold Him to be all-powerful, and even the peoples Western writers label "savages" or "primitives", for whom "degenerates" would be the truer word, hold some vague idea of a supreme deity and usually quite vivid ideas about the next world. The Qur'an lets none of this pass for faith. Faith in Allah is valid and deserves the name only when it conforms to what the Qur'an lays down about the divine names and attributes, and belief in the Hereafter is valid only when it matches what the Qur'an and the hadith specify. Books are made without end, and so are gods and names for gods, never more than in modern times. Reason, Nature, Man and Life, having served their turn and grown rusty, are being replaced by fancier names, "the ground of being", the "archetype of the collective unconscious", and lately even a godless theology. Measured by these requirements, the Jews who posed as Muslims believed in neither Allah nor the Hereafter. They took the prophet ʿUzayr (Ezra) for the son of God, and they fondly believed that the prophets' descendants, whatever they did, would stay God's chosen people and escape the reckoning of the Day of Judgment, or at worst suffer a token punishment. Holding such beliefs, their claim to faith in Allah and the Hereafter was rightly rejected.

Verse 13 defines faith: believe as other people have believed. The standard for judging any claim to faith is the faith of the Companions, and a claim that does not conform to it is not accepted by Allah or His Prophet ﷺ. If someone presumes, as is all too common nowadays, to interpret an Islamic doctrine or a verse of the Qur'an in a way that departs from the clear explanation given by the Qur'an itself or by the Prophet ﷺ, his private opinion, however much it pleases his contemporaries or feeds their fancy, has no value or validity in the Sharīʿah. For example, the Qadianis, who style themselves Ahmadis, claim that like Muslims they believe in the finality of the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ, but they depart from what the Prophet ﷺ himself stated and the Companions believed, and twist the doctrine until it has room for Mirza Ghulam Ahmad of Qadian as a prophet, so by the Qur'an's indication the same verdict falls on them: they are not believers. To sum up, when a man reads an Islamic doctrine in a way that clashes with the faith of the Companions and still claims to be a Muslim on the strength of that doctrine, performing his religious duties exactly like Muslims, he is not counted a believer until he agrees to conform to the criterion of faith the Qur'an has laid down.

This also clears up a misunderstanding, often raised and more often raised on purpose, about the well-known rule in hadith and fiqh that the "people of the qiblah", those who face the Kaʿbah in the prescribed prayer, may not be branded disbelievers. These verses define the phrase. It applies only to those who deny none of the essential doctrines and commandments of Islam, the ḍarūriyyāt. The hypocrites mentioned in the Qur'an prayed exactly as the Muslims did, yet facing the Kaʿbah was not taken as enough to make them true Muslims, simply because they did not believe in all the essentials of Islam as the Companions did.

### Belonging to neither side

The hypocrites wanted to keep their ties with the disbelievers while mixing with the Muslims. Before the Muslims they said, "We are with you," and alone with their own kind among the disbelievers they voiced their loyalty to them. They wanted relationships with both sides, and were shut out of both: "Torn between belief and disbelief—belonging neither to these ˹believers˺ nor those ˹disbelievers˺" (4:143). The inner reading extends this to anyone who wants to combine the path of spiritual desire with the habits of ordinary people. It cannot be done, because two opposites do not combine. The slave who has contracted with his master for his freedom remains a slave until the last dirham is paid. When night draws near, day slips away. Whoever keeps a mixed crowd in every corner and a heart tied to every nook is headed for ruin. One group after another takes its turn living in his heart, so that it is forever wrecked, and he gets no pleasure from life and no real provision from his heart. In the words of a poet about such people: I see you as a leftover from the people of Mūsā (Moses), for they would not wait patiently for their food.

In a dark room black and white look the same, but turn on the light and black shows as black and white as white. So it is with the message Allah revealed to the prophets. The divine scriptures are His beacons to the world, and when their light falls on mankind, guidance and error appear for what they are, and so do good and evil deeds and their consequences. But some people do not bow to the truth. They want the truth to serve them, and Allah's light only confuses them. Hidden jealousy and pride take hold of them, and the moment they see themselves in the divine mirror their resentments are stirred and their prejudices overwhelm their senses.

### In short

- The hypocrites professed faith to the believers for safety and advantage, then told their leaders, the "devils", human and jinn, that it was all mockery. ʿAbdullāh ibn Ubayy's staged greeting of Abū Bakr, ʿUmar and ʿAlī was the occasion of the verse.
- Their profession, "We believe in Allah and the Last Day", was rejected because faith counts only when it matches what the Qur'an and the Prophet ﷺ laid down and what the Companions believed. That standard excludes anyone who reshapes an essential doctrine, and it defines who the "people of the qiblah" are.
- Wanting both camps, they ended up in neither, which is the fate of anyone who tries to join the way of Allah with the way of the crowd.

15.text:
The answer to "we were only mocking" comes from Allah Himself. "Allah will throw their mockery back at them, leaving them to continue wandering blindly in their defiance". The hypocrites were delighted with themselves, sure they could make fools of the Muslims and get away with it. Allah gave them a long rope, and the rope was the punishment.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Allah will throw their mockery back at them"** means He requites them for their mockery, repaying them in equal measure. Ibn Jarīr pointed to what Allah will do with them on the Day of Resurrection: "On that Day hypocrite men and women will beg the believers, “Wait for us so that we may have some of your light.” It will be said ˹mockingly˺, “Go back ˹to the world˺ and seek a light ˹there˺!”" (57:13), and "Those who disbelieve should not think that living longer is good for them. They are only given more time to increase in sin, and they will suffer a humiliating punishment" (3:178). This, he said, and things like it, is Allah's mockery of the hypocrites and the people of shirk. One description of it: in the Hereafter a gate of Paradise is opened to them and then shut in their faces, while the believers laugh. In this world they are treated as believers, and in the next they are repaid for their lying and deception.

Allah describes the deed and its punishment with the same word, though the meanings differ, just as He said, "The reward of an evil deed is its equivalent" (42:40), and "if anyone attacks you, retaliate in the same manner" (2:194). The first act is injustice and the second is justice. The two share a name but differ in reality. This is how the scholars explain deceit, cunning and mockery whenever they are attributed to Allah in the Qur'an. He takes revenge for certain evil acts with a punishment that matches the act in kind. By consensus of the scholars He does none of this in play. It is a just punishment for particular evil deeds.

**"leaving them to continue wandering blindly in their defiance"** means that He gives them respite, as Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd and several other Companions explained through as-Suddī. Mujāhid said it means He increases them in their deviation. Both are in the Qur'an: "Do they think, since We provide them with wealth and children, that We hasten to ˹honour˺ them ˹with˺ all kinds of good? No! They are not aware" (23:55-56). Ibn Jarīr took the correct meaning to be as in "We turn their hearts and eyes away ˹from the truth˺ as they refused to believe at first, leaving them to wander blindly in their defiance" (6:110). Ṭughyān, "defiance", means transgressing the limits, as the water did in "when the floodwater had overflowed, We carried you in the floating Ark" (69:11), and here it is the limits of disbelief that they overstep. Ibn Jarīr said the word for wandering, ʿamah, means deviation, and explained the phrase: in the misguidance and disbelief that have surrounded them they are confused and cannot find a way out, because Allah has stamped and sealed their hearts and blinded their sight, so they neither recognise guidance nor find the exit from their error. The final word, yaʿmahūn, describes their state: wavering in perplexity, left in this world blind in their disbelief, unable to see faith or guidance, more and more lost, doing more and more wrong, confused and doubtful about the truth.

### How the mockery worked

The hypocrites were mightily pleased with themselves for fooling the Muslims, when they were only fooling themselves. Allah, in His forbearance and mercy, gave them a long rope, and that very rope was the means of making them ridiculous. Seeing no visible sign of divine punishment coming down on them, they grew bolder in their complacency and rebellion, until the cup of their wickedness was full and one day they were caught. Allah acted this way in response to their mockery, so the Qur'an calls His action mockery too.

### The inner reading

When people put the reins in the hands of their desires they are lured into the valleys of separation. Their feet find no firm place, and they wander in the maze of absence. Just as Allah leaves the hypocrites bewildered in their defiance, He prolongs the time they spend with their muddled hopes, so that when death approaches their hopes have never been higher and their deeds never lower. That is their repayment for what they did, the poisonous fruit of their own making. The worst of their punishments is that their ugly deeds look beautiful to them, and their greatest misfortune is that they are content with their lethargy.

### In short

- Allah's "mockery" is the just repayment of their mockery, named after the crime as retaliation is named after the offence. It is never play.
- It takes the form of respite in this world, which lets them fill their cup, and of humiliation in the next, when they beg for the believers' light and are turned back.
- Their defiance is overstepping the bounds of disbelief, and their wandering is the blindness of sealed hearts that cannot find the way out.

16.text:
The hypocrites thought of themselves as shrewd men of the world. The Qur'an judges them as traders. "They are the ones who trade guidance for misguidance. But this trade is profitless, and they are not ˹rightly˺ guided". They gave away the most valuable thing there is for something worthless and even harmful, and in calling that a trade the verse implies that these worldly-wise men did not understand even the art of trading.

### Phrase by phrase

**"They are the ones who trade guidance for misguidance"** means, as Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Masʿūd said through as-Suddī, that they took up misguidance and abandoned guidance. Mujāhid said they believed and then disbelieved. Qatādah said they preferred error to guidance, which matches what Allah said of Thamūd: "As for Thamûd, We showed them guidance, but they preferred blindness over guidance" (41:17). Taken together, these explanations show that the hypocrites turned from true guidance and chose misguidance, putting wickedness in the place of righteousness. They exchanged guidance to buy error, choosing disbelief instead of faith. The verse covers both those who first believed and later disbelieved, of whom Allah said, "This is because they believed and then abandoned faith. Therefore, their hearts have been sealed, so they do not comprehend" (63:3), and those who simply preferred deviation over guidance, for the hypocrites are of several kinds.

**"But this trade is profitless"** means their dealing did not succeed. They gained nothing from it and in fact lost, since their destination is the Fire, made everlasting for them. The exchange of faith for disbelief helped them in no way, because they lost their faith in Allah and lost the road to the truth. In this they showed themselves the real fools.

**"and they are not ˹rightly˺ guided"** means they were neither righteous nor rightly guided in any of this, and they were not guided to a way out of their error. Ibn Jarīr recorded Qatādah's comment: "By Allah, I have seen them leave guidance for error, leave the community for the sects, leave safety for fear, and leave the Sunnah for innovation." Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported similar statements.

### A failure of ordinary judgment

The verse shows the hypocrites' basic dullness. They failed to use the ordinary power of telling things apart. Raised in a pagan society, they knew perfectly well what the disbelievers' way was, and by now they were familiar enough with Islam to see the difference easily. Yet out of greed, for petty worldly profit, they still chose disbelief over Islam, bartering something as priceless as faith for something as worthless and harmful as disbelief.

### The inner reading

The verse alludes to those who have neglected what they owe by staying in the familiar territory of worldly fortunes. They have lost their bargain. Whoever is content with this world over the next is in plain loss. Whoever prefers this world, or the next, over the Real suffers the most intense loss of all. The one who loses the gardens of bliss falls short, but the one who truly suffers is the one afflicted with distance from intimate conversation with his Protector, whose heart has been cut loose from Him, who stays captive to his desires with no messenger reaching his heart, whose spirit attains nothing, with no intimate speech, no approach and no witnessing within. If even a moment slips from him, his Lord has slipped from him, and moments have no substitutes. As a poet said: you were the pupil of my eye, and the eye I see with wept for you; let anyone who still has a will after you die, for I used to stand guard over you.

### In short

- The hypocrites swapped guidance for error, some by believing and then disbelieving, some by preferring blindness as Thamūd did.
- It was a losing trade: nothing gained, faith and the way to truth lost, and the Fire at the end.
- Men who prided themselves on worldly shrewdness showed they could not tell a good bargain from a ruinous one.

17.text:
The surah now paints the hypocrites in a picture. "Their example is that of someone who kindles a fire, but when it lights up all around them, Allah takes away their light, leaving them in complete darkness—unable to see". Two extended similes close the portrait, this one of fire and the next of water, and they describe two kinds of hypocrite. This verse is about the kind in whom disbelief had taken deep root, who had little inclination toward Islam and pretended to be Muslims for worldly motives: the man who found light and lost it again.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Their example is that of someone who kindles a fire"** describes how the hypocrites stand in their hypocrisy. A man lights a fire in the darkness, at the beginning of the night, to keep his person, family and property safe. Though the verse speaks of one man, the pronoun that follows is plural, "their light", because the Arabic alladhī here carries a plural sense.
