**"but when it lights up all around them"** means that when the fire is lit and illuminates the area around him, so that he can see, feel warm and feel secure from whatever he feared, at that very moment it is put out.

**"Allah takes away their light"** means He removes what benefits them, the light, and leaves them what harms them, the darkness and the smoke. He extinguishes it.

**"leaving them in complete darkness—unable to see"** means that total darkness falls on this man and he cannot see anything around him or find his way out. He is confused about the road and afraid. The darkness is their doubts, disbelief and hypocrisy, and not seeing means being unable to find the right path or even its direction.

### What the picture means

When the hypocrites bought error with guidance they acquired utter blindness, and this is their likeness. The man benefited from his fire and felt safe, then it suddenly went out and he was left in the dark. Worse, he cannot hear or speak, and he has become so blind that even if there were light he could not see, so he can never return to the state he was in before. Such are the hypocrites who preferred misguidance to guidance and deviation to righteousness. The parable indicates that they first believed and then disbelieved, as the Qur'an says of them elsewhere. In practical terms, the hypocrites professed belief in Muhammad ﷺ and the Qur'an openly and so felt that their persons, families and property were safe, escaping imprisonment or death. But when they die Allah takes away the benefit of that outward faith and leaves them in the darkness of the grave's hardships, where they see no comfort. People who have bought temporary security by professing faith will meet terror and punishment at death. Something of this world's benefits appears to them outwardly, and then the pain of the punishment overtakes them in the Hereafter. Or, in another reading, a flash of affirmation appears in them, and then they remain in the darkness of their denial.

It is also said that the simile refers to the Jews. Their situation with regard to Muhammad ﷺ was that of a man who, in a lost battle, raises a flag and gathers the other defeated fighters to it, then lowers it once they have gathered, so that the benefit and safety it offered vanish at once. Before the Qur'an was revealed the Jews used to say that Muhammad ﷺ and the Qur'an would support them, and when it came they denied it, so Allah took away their light, their desire to believe and the benefit it would have brought. Though they wanted to believe in him they did not, and they were left in the error of their religion, unable to see guidance.

The hypocrites are also warned in these parables that they are not beyond Allah's power. He can take away their sight and hearing whenever He wills, and even destroy them.

### The objection to parables

When Allah struck these two similitudes for the hypocrites, this one and the one about the rainstorm from the sky (2:19), the hypocrites said, as Ibn ʿAbbās reported through Abū Ṣāliḥ, that Allah is too exalted and sublime to coin similitudes, and Allah sent down the verse "Surely Allah does not shy away from using the parable of a mosquito or what is even smaller" (2:26). Al-Ḥasan and Qatādah said that when gnats and spiders appeared in Allah's Book as similitudes for the disbelievers, the Jews laughed and said this did not resemble Allah's speech, and so that verse came down. Through Ibn Jurayj from ʿAṭāʾ, Ibn ʿAbbās explained that Allah had mentioned the idolaters' gods, saying, "if a fly were to snatch anything away from them, they cannot ˹even˺ retrieve it" (22:73), and had compared their scheme to a cobweb, and the idolaters said, "See how Allah mentions gnats and spiders in the Qur'an revealed to Muhammad. What is the use of this?" The verse answered them.

### The seeker who turns back

In the inner reading, the verse alludes to a person who makes a beautiful beginning on the path of spiritual desire. He toils for a time and bears one hardship after another, then returns to the world before reaching the truth and falls back into the darkness of his own nature. His stem sprouted but bore no fruit. His branch blossomed but never ripened. He hurried on the eclipse of lethargy over the moons of Allah's presence, and the hand of subjugation rejected him after the tongue of kindness had beckoned him. His heart moved away from nearness, and his lower self filled with rancour toward the seekers. As the poet says, when passion settled in and we called ourselves happy, we thought ourselves safe from growing apart, but division sent its messengers in secret and destroyed what our union had built. The verse also alludes to the one who grasps only the lowest level of understanding yet makes claims far above it: when the increase in his states is cut off he is left in the darkness of his claims. And it alludes to the one who leans on the rubble and glitter of this world. When his affairs have settled into a well-worn road, hope and rising expectation carrying him along, death springs on him as an ambush of the divine ruse. He leaves everything behind and carries the burden forward.

### In short

- The hypocrite is a man who lit a fire for safety and had it snuffed out the moment it began to serve him. His profession of faith secured him in this world, and death takes that light away.
- The simile points to those who believed and then disbelieved, and by another reading to the Jews who awaited a prophet and denied him when he came.
- The parables drew mockery, and Allah answered it in verse 26: He does not shy away from any example, however small.

18.text:
The parable ends with a verdict on the man left in the dark. "They are ˹wilfully˺ deaf, dumb, and blind, so they will never return ˹to the Right Path˺". Three senses are named, and the loss of all three explains why there is no way back.

### Phrase by phrase

**"They are ˹wilfully˺ deaf"** means they cannot hear the guidance. They are deaf to the truth, unable to hear it and accept it, and they behave as if they were deaf.

**"dumb"** means they cannot utter the words that would benefit them. They are mute where goodness is concerned, unable to speak of it, and they act as if they were dumb.

**"and blind"** means they are in total darkness and deviation, blind to the path of guidance so that they cannot see it, and they act as if they were blind. Allah said, "it is not the eyes that are blind, but it is the hearts in the chests that grow blind" (22:46).

**"so they will never return ˹to the Right Path˺"** means they cannot get back to the guidance they once had, because they sold it for misguidance. They do not turn back from their disbelief and error.

### Senses that refuse to work

People of this kind have eyes but do not see, ears but do not hear, tongues but do not speak. They can neither hear the call of truth, nor answer it in any way, nor find their way by any sign from Allah. Instead of reflecting on the call as they should, they dodge it, either by treating it as unimportant or by not listening at all.

### The inner reading

Their hearts' ears are deaf to the Real's calls. The tongue of their innermost self is dumb, unable to converse with Him in whispers. The eyes of their insight are blind to the flow of decreed events. They do not turn back from their persistent shamelessness, and nothing deters them from the error they have embraced with their whole heart. Another way of putting it: they cannot hear through the Real, cannot speak through the Real, and cannot study creation through the Real. Nothing was decreed for them that would make them desist, and no share was allotted to them that would help them be deterred.

### In short

- Deaf to guidance, dumb about anything good, blind to the way: the three channels by which truth reaches a person are all shut.
- The blindness is of the heart, not the eyes, and it is wilful, a pretence that became a condition.
- Having sold their guidance, they have nothing to return to, and so they do not return.

19.text:
A second picture follows the fire. "Or ˹those caught in˺ a rainstorm from the sky with darkness, thunder, and lightning. They press their fingers into their ears at the sound of every thunder-clap for fear of death. And Allah encompasses the disbelievers ˹by His might˺". The first simile was fire. This one is water: travellers caught at night in a downpour, with darkness around them, thunder overhead and lightning flashing. It describes the hypocrites who sometimes know the truth and at other times doubt it, the ones who recognised Islam and even wished at times to be real Muslims, but whose worldly interests would not let them, so that they lived in a permanent state of hesitation and doubt.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Or ˹those caught in˺ a rainstorm from the sky"** means that their likeness is that of people out in heavy rain. The Arabic ṣayyib is rain, as Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās and several other Companions confirmed. Among the next generations the same was said by Qatādah, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Mujāhid, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, as-Suddī, ʿAṭāʾ, ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī and ʿAṭiyah al-ʿAwfī. Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk said it is the clouds, but the accepted view is the rain. The word comes from a verb meaning "to come down", and "from the sky" means from the clouds. The rain stands for the Qur'an, which came down from Allah, pouring at night onto open country.

**"with darkness, thunder, and lightning"** describes the storm: darkness layer upon layer, thunder, and lightning. In the parable, the darkness is the hypocrites' doubts, disbelief and hypocrisy, the thunder is what shocks their hearts with fear, and the lightning is the light of faith that sometimes glimmers in them. Read as a picture of the Qur'an, the darkness is its account of disbelief and of trials, the thunder is its rebukes and threats of punishment, and the lightning is its clear arguments, its exposition, instruction and promise. One opinion holds that the thunder is the angel in charge of the clouds, or the sound of his voice, and the lightning the flash of that voice as he drives the clouds along.

**"They press their fingers into their ears at the sound of every thunder-clap for fear of death"** means that people caught in such a storm stop their ears with their fingertips against the violent crash of thunder, afraid that hearing it might kill them. So it was with the Jews and the hypocrites when the Qur'an was recited with its promises and threats falling like thunder-claps. They stopped their ears so as not to hear it and be drawn toward faith and away from their own religion, which to them would have been death. The hypocrites are generally full of fear and anxiety, as Allah described them: "They think every cry is against them" (63:4), and "They swear by Allah that they are part of you, but they are not. They only say so out of fear. If only they could find a refuge, or a cave, or any hiding-place, they would rush headlong towards it" (9:56-57).

**"And Allah encompasses the disbelievers ˹by His might˺"** means that their caution does them no good, because they are held within Allah's all-embracing will and decree. He encompasses them in knowledge and in power, so they cannot escape Him. He knows them and will gather them in Hell. The same was said of earlier tyrants: "Has the story of the ˹destroyed˺ forces reached you ˹O Prophet˺—" of Firʿawn (Pharaoh) and Thamūd, "But Allah encompasses them from all sides" (85:17-20).

### Fear as a barrier

Fear is another thing that keeps people from acknowledging the truth. Rain is a wonderful blessing, but thunder and lightning come with it and terrify the faint-hearted. The word of Allah revealed to His prophets works on them in the same way. It holds out the promise of great success, and at the same time accepting it puts a person temporarily at risk: the fear of losing one's worldly position, of clashing with the established order. Fear of these things sometimes stops a person dead and sometimes makes him move forward hesitantly. Such caution cannot help him. Those who do not answer Allah's call open-heartedly are deprived of His blessings in this world and the next. The hypocrites resemble the people in both parables because they get nothing of value from either: from the fire only darkness and smouldering embers, from the storm-cloud only fear and alarm at the thunder and lightning. In the same way they saw nothing in Islam but difficulty and harshness.

### The inner reading

The "or" means that either of the two similitudes may be applied to them. The Qur'an is compared to rain falling from the sky, and its promises and threats to the thunder and lightning in the rain. Their taking refuge, their flight from hearing the Qur'an, their avoidance of attention and their refusal to seek insight, is compared to people stopping their ears against the thunder. The allusion extends to the heedless, whenever a warner's admonition reaches their ears or a light of felicity falls on their hearts. If they would stop their blind heedlessness they would be happy. Instead they keep one another distracted with false hopes and are set on their corrupt road. They make weak excuses, "And they will swear by Allah, “Had we been able, we would have certainly joined you.” They are ruining themselves" (9:42), and bring about their ruin with their own hands. When a noble person gives you his love he veils what is ugly and brings out what is beautiful. In the same way, when someone grows tired and wants to break things off he wearies of being together and says, "That was that."

### In short

- The hypocrites of this verse are not the hardened kind but the wavering kind, who see the truth in flashes and lose it again.
- The rain is the Qur'an, the darkness is doubt and disbelief, the thunder is its warnings and the lightning its light. Stopping the ears is refusing to listen for fear of where listening leads.
- Fear of worldly loss is a real barrier to faith, but the caution it produces is useless, because Allah encompasses the disbelievers on every side.

20.text:
The storm picture continues, and now the travellers move. "It is as if the lightning were about to snatch away their sight. Whenever lightning strikes, they walk in its light, but when darkness covers them, they stand still. Had Allah willed, He could have taken away their hearing and sight. Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything". A step or two in each flash, then a halt in the dark. That is the hesitant hypocrite, and the verse ends by reminding him that his remaining senses are his only by Allah's leave.

### Phrase by phrase

**"It is as if the lightning were about to snatch away their sight"** means that it all but takes their sight away in an instant, both because the lightning is so strong and because their understanding is so weak that it cannot bear the faith. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah reported Ibn ʿAbbās's comment that the Qur'an laid bare almost all the secrets of the hypocrites. In the allegorical reading, the exposition of the Qur'an all but snatched away their error.

**"Whenever lightning strikes, they walk in its light"** means that whenever it flashes they walk by it. Through ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah, Ibn ʿAbbās explained: whenever the hypocrites get a share in the victories of Islam they are content with it, and whenever Islam suffers a setback they are ready to go back to disbelief, as Allah said, "there are some who worship Allah on the verge ˹of faith˺: if they are blessed with something good, they are content with it; but if they are afflicted with a trial, they relapse ˹into disbelief˺, losing this world and the Hereafter" (22:11). Through Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq, Ibn ʿAbbās said that they recognise the truth and speak of it, so that their speech is upright, and then they go back to disbelief and fall into confusion again. Abū al-ʿĀliyah, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Qatādah, ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas and as-Suddī said the same, reporting it from the Companions, and it is the clearest and most correct view. Allah knows best. The simile pictures the turmoil the Qur'an's arguments stir in their hearts: they acknowledge the truths they like hearing and recoil from what they detest. In worldly terms, when the hypocrites declared themselves believers they went along with whatever the believers went along with, because their outward faith was accepted.

**"but when darkness covers them, they stand still"** means they stop and stay in the dark. When they die they remain in the darkness of the grave.

**"Had Allah willed, He could have taken away their hearing and sight"** means their outward hearing and sight, as He had already taken away their inner ones. Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq reported Ibn ʿAbbās's explanation: because they abandoned the truth after knowing it. In the allegorical reading, He could take away the thunder and the lightning, that is, their hearing of the Qur'an's rebukes and threats and their sight of its exposition, and not give them back, since they turn from the truth.

**"Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything"** means that He is able to punish or pardon His servants as He wills, as Ibn ʿAbbās said. Ibn Jarīr commented that Allah describes Himself here as able to do everything in order to warn the hypocrites of His control over all things and to tell them that His power completely encompasses them and that He can take away their hearing and their sight. The parables thus carry a warning: the hypocrites are not beyond Allah's power, and He can remove their sight and hearing, or destroy them, whenever He wills.

### Light on the Day of Judgment

On the Day of Judgment the believers will be given light in proportion to their faith. Some will have light that shines for miles, some more and some less. Some people's light will glow at times and go out at times, and they will walk on the Ṣirāṭ, the bridge over the Fire, while it shines and stop when it goes out. Some will have no light at all, and these are the hypocrites: "On that Day hypocrite men and women will beg the believers, “Wait for us so that we may have some of your light.” It will be said ˹mockingly˺, “Go back ˹to the world˺ and seek a light ˹there˺!”" (57:13). Of the believers Allah said, "On that Day you will see believing men and women with their light shining ahead of them and on their right" (57:12), and "on the Day Allah will not disgrace the Prophet or the believers with him. Their light will shine ahead of them and on their right. They will say, “Our Lord! Perfect our light for us”" (66:8). Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd's comment on the light running ahead of them: they will cross the Ṣirāṭ according to their deeds, some with a light the size of a mountain, some with a light the size of a date palm, and the people with the least light will have it on their index fingers, lit one moment and out the next. Ibn Abī Ḥātim also recorded Ibn ʿAbbās saying that every person of tawḥīd will receive a light on the Day of Resurrection, and the hypocrite's light will go out, and when the believers see that they will be anxious and pray, "Our Lord! Perfect our light for us." Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Muzāḥim said the same: everyone who embraced faith will be given a light, and when they reach the Ṣirāṭ the hypocrites' light will be extinguished, and the believers, seeing it, will make that prayer.

### The kinds of people the surah has described

The opening of the surah has now sorted people into kinds. There are the believers of verses 2 to 5. There are the disbelievers of the two verses after them. And there are two categories of hypocrite: the complete hypocrites of the fire parable, and the hesitant hypocrites, in whom the light of faith flickers on and off, for whom the rain parable was revealed and who are less evil than the first. This resembles the parables of Sūrat an-Nūr, where the believer and the faith Allah placed in his heart are likened to a brightly lit lamp like a rising star, a heart built on faith and nourished by the revealed law without impurity or flaw. Then the disbelievers who think they have something when they have nothing, the people of compound ignorance, are given their parable: "As for the disbelievers, their deeds are like a mirage in a desert, which the thirsty perceive as water" (24:39). Then the simple, ignorant disbelievers: "Or ˹their deeds are˺ like the darkness in a deep sea, covered by waves upon waves, topped by ˹dark˺ clouds" (24:40). So Allah divided the disbelievers into leaders and followers, and He named both at the start of Sūrat al-Ḥajj, "there are some who dispute about Allah without knowledge, and follow every rebellious devil" (22:3), and "there are some who dispute about Allah without knowledge, guidance, or an enlightening scripture" (22:8). He divided the believers too, at the beginning and end of Sūrat al-Wāqiʿah and in Sūrat al-Insān, into the foremost, who are the near ones, and the companions of the right, who are the righteous.

In sum, the believers are of two kinds, the near ones and the righteous. The disbelievers are of two kinds, leaders and followers. And the hypocrites are of two kinds, the pure hypocrites and those with some hypocrisy in them. The two Ṣaḥīḥs record from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr that the Prophet ﷺ said that whoever has three traits is a pure hypocrite, and whoever has one of them has one trait of hypocrisy until he gives it up: when he speaks he lies, when he makes a pact he betrays it, and when he is trusted he breaks the trust. So a person may have a portion of faith and a portion of hypocrisy at once, in conduct, as this hadith states, or in belief, as this verse indicates.

Imām Aḥmad recorded from Abū Saʿīd that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said hearts are of four kinds: a polished heart shining like a radiant lamp, a sealed heart with a knot tied over its seal, a heart turned upside down, and a wrapped heart. The polished heart is the believer's, and its lamp is the light of faith. The sealed heart is the disbeliever's. The upside-down heart is the pure hypocrite's, because he knew and then denied. The wrapped heart holds both faith and hypocrisy. Faith in it is like a herb fed by pure water, and hypocrisy in it is like an ulcer fed by pus and blood, and whichever of the two gets the upper hand takes the heart. The chain of this hadith is good, jayyid ḥasan.

### One parable or two?

Ibn Jarīr and several other scholars held that both parables are about the same kind of hypocrite, so that the "or" of "Or ˹those caught in˺ a rainstorm" means "and", as in the verse telling the Prophet ﷺ to obey neither a sinner nor a disbeliever among them, and the "or" offers a choice of either example. Al-Qurṭubī said the "or" shows that the two choices are equivalent, as when one says, "Sit with al-Ḥasan or Ibn Sīrīn," which in az-Zamakhsharī's explanation means that each is as good as the other, so you may sit with either, and the "or" comes to mean "either". On that view Allah gave two examples because both describe the hypocrites perfectly. Another view, however, is that the two descriptions belong to two types of hypocrite, since there is a difference between them. Allah distinguished their types in Sūrat Barāʾah, chapter 9, by repeating "and among them" three times to describe their kinds, traits, sayings and deeds. So the two examples here describe two types whose characteristics are similar, just as Sūrat an-Nūr gives two examples of disbelief, the mirage for its leaders, who have compound ignorance, and the darkness of the deep sea for its followers, who have simple ignorance. Allah knows best.

### The inner reading

The similitude also fits the heedless. When they sit at public sermons, or their hearts soften, or some terror overwhelms them, their states move toward repentance and their longing to turn to Allah grows strong. Then they go back to their own planning and consult those close to them, and their family and children urge them back to their world, frightening them with weakness and dependence, until their resolve weakens and their spiritual desire declines. As the saying goes, whenever he repents he returns to his ignorance, as a feeble man relapses. "Had Allah willed, He could have taken away their hearing and sight" refers to the hypocrites' outward hearing and sight, in addition to their inner deafness and blindness. The same holds for the heedless and for those content with the outward side of Islam: Allah has the power to cancel the fruit of their outward acts of obedience, just as He has the power to cancel the realisation of whatever they have tasted of the most felicitous states.

### In short

- The wavering hypocrite walks when faith flashes and stops when it fades, content when Islam prospers and ready to turn back when it is tested.
- This hesitation has an exact counterpart on the Day of Judgment, when light is given by faith and the hypocrites' light goes out on the bridge.
- The surah has now described six kinds of people: two kinds of believer, two kinds of disbeliever and two kinds of hypocrite. A person may carry a part of faith and a part of hypocrisy at once.
- Whether the two parables describe one type or two, their last word is the same: Allah encompasses the hypocrites and could take their hearing and sight at any moment.

21.text:
After describing the three kinds of people, the surah speaks to all of them at once. "O humanity! Worship your Lord, Who created you and those before you, so that you may become mindful ˹of Him˺". This is the first command in the Qur'an's order of arrangement, and it carries the message for which the whole Book was sent down: give up the worship of created things and worship the Creator alone. The verse does not simply assert this. It argues it, in a sentence so short and so clear that an ordinary person using ordinary common sense cannot help being convinced.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O humanity!"** translates an-nās, mankind in general, so the address takes in all three groups just described: the believers, the disbelievers and the hypocrites. It is also understood as addressed to the people of Makkah, and some say to the Jews. Alqamah laid down a rule, reported through al-Aʿmash and Ibrāhīm, that whatever revelation contains "O mankind" is Makkan and whatever contains "O you who believe" is Madinan, meaning that the first is addressed to the people of Makkah and the second to the people of Madinah. On that basis this verse addresses the idolaters of Makkah, and the address to them runs on until "Give good news ˹O Prophet˺ to those who believe" (2:25), which was revealed about the believers, because Allah wished to mention the reward of the believers after mentioning the reward of the disbelievers in "the Fire fuelled with people and stones, which is prepared for the disbelievers" (2:24).

**"Worship your Lord"** means profess His oneness and worship no one but Him. ʿIbādah, worship, means spending every energy one has in total obedience to someone and shunning all disobedience out of awe and reverence for him. The choice of the name Rabb, the One who nurtures, from among Allah's beautiful names is deliberate, because it folds the argument into the command. The Rabb is the final and absolute cause of a human being's nurture, the One who takes him by gradual stages from a drop of fluid to a healthy, feeling, reasoning person and who provides the means of his sustenance and growth. This is so obvious that even a dull or ignorant man, on a little reflection, would see that only Allah, and no created being, can have such a power. What can a creature do for a man when its own existence is owed to the Creator? Can one needy being rescue another? If it seems to, the nurturing in reality belongs to the One Being on whom both depend in order to exist at all. So who but the Rabb deserves adoration and worship?

The command means something different to each group it addresses. To the disbelievers it says: stop worshipping created beings and turn to the Creator. To the hypocrites: be sincere and true in your faith. To sinning Muslims: change your ways and perfect your obedience. To the mindful Muslims: stay steadfast in worship and obedience and strive harder in Allah's way.

**"Who created you and those before you"** names a quality that no one could even imagine belonging to a created being: giving existence to what did not exist, making you when you were nothing, and bringing out of the darkness and uncleanness of the womb a creature as lovely and noble as a human being. He created you in your different lineages, beginning from a drop of sperm, just as He created those who came before you. Adding "and those before you" makes Him the sole Creator of the whole human race. It is also telling that the verse speaks of those before you and says nothing of those who will come after. The silence hints that no community will succeed the community of the Prophet ﷺ, because no prophet will be sent after the Last Prophet ﷺ and so no new ummah will arise.

**"so that you may become mindful ˹of Him˺"** can also be rendered "so that you may save yourselves from Hell" or "so that you may guard yourselves against evil": so that you may ward off His anger and punishment by obeying Him, following His instructions and keeping away from what He has forbidden. The point is that salvation and Paradise can be hoped for only by worshipping Allah alone and associating nothing with Him. An important doctrinal point lies in the particle laʿalla, "so that ... may", which expresses expectation or hope and is used where it is not definite that something will happen. A person who truly has faith and truly believes in Allah's oneness will certainly attain salvation and Paradise, as Allah Himself has promised. The certainty is expressed here as a hope to make a person realise that no human act, by itself, can earn salvation as a necessary reward. Salvation and Paradise come by the grace of Allah alone. The ability to do good, and faith itself, are signs of divine grace, not its cause. When Allah uses this hopeful word, it carries the force of an affirmation. In the inner reading, the word brings the command closer to people and makes it lighter, and keeps them between fear and hope.

### Where the verse stands

The second verse of the surah answered the prayer of al-Fātiḥah, "Guide us along the Straight Path": the guidance asked for is in this Book, which from beginning to end is a detailed account of the straight path. The surah then divided people into three groups by their acceptance or rejection of that guidance: the true, mindful Muslims who accept it and act on it, the disbelievers who oppose it openly, and the hypocrites who are hostile to it but hide their disbelief, for petty worldly interest or to harm the Muslims, and present themselves as Muslims. In sorting people this way the first twenty verses show that the right basis for dividing mankind is neither race nor colour, neither language nor geography, but religion. Those who believe in Allah and follow His guidance in the Qur'an form one nation and those who disbelieve form another. The Qur'an calls the first the party of Allah and the second the party of Shayṭān: "They are the party of Satan. Surely Satan's party is bound to lose" (58:19-22). Now verses 21 and 22, addressing all three groups together, present the message itself.

### The hadith on Allah's right

The two Ṣaḥīḥs record that Ibn Masʿūd asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ which sin is the gravest with Allah, and he answered: that you set up an equal to Allah when He alone created you. Muʿādh narrated the Prophet's ﷺ words: do you know what Allah's right over His servants is? That they worship Him alone and associate nothing with Him. Another hadith says that none of you should say, "What Allah wills and so-and-so wills," but rather, "What Allah wills, and then what so-and-so wills."

Imām Aḥmad recorded from al-Ḥārith al-Ashʿarī that the Prophet ﷺ said that Allah commanded Yaḥyā ibn Zakariyyā to carry out five commands and to order the Children of Israel to carry them out, and Yaḥyā was slow about it. ʿĪsā (Jesus) said to him: you were ordered five commands and to order the Children of Israel with them, so either you give the order or I will. Yaḥyā said, "My brother, I fear that if you do it before me I will be punished, or the earth will be made to shake under my feet." So Yaḥyā gathered the Children of Israel in Bayt al-Maqdis in Jerusalem until they filled the masjid. He sat on a raised place, thanked and praised Allah, and said that Allah had ordered him five commands and ordered him to order them with them. The first was to worship Allah alone and associate nothing with Him. The likeness of this, he said, is a man who buys a servant with his own money, in silver or gold, and the servant works but hands the earnings to someone else. Which of you would be pleased with such a servant? Allah created you and sustains you, so worship Him alone and associate nothing with Him. He also commanded them to pray, because Allah keeps His face turned toward the face of His servant for as long as the servant does not look away, so do not turn your heads this way and that in prayer. He commanded them to fast, whose likeness is a man in a company of men carrying musk wrapped in a cloth, so that everyone smells it, for the breath of the fasting person is better with Allah than the scent of musk. He commanded them to give charity, whose likeness is a man captured by the enemy, his hands tied to his neck, brought forward to be beheaded, who asks whether he may ransom himself and keeps paying small sums and large until he frees himself. And he commanded them to remember Allah always, whose likeness is a man pursued hard by the enemy who takes refuge in a strong fortress, for when the servant remembers Allah he has taken the best refuge from Shayṭān. Al-Ḥārith went on to relate the Prophet's ﷺ own addition: and I order you with five that Allah ordered me: keep to the community, listen and obey, and perform hijrah and jihād in the way of Allah. Whoever leaves the community by so much as a hand-span has removed the tie of Islam from his neck unless he returns, and whoever uses the slogans of the days of ignorance will be among those kneeling in Jahannam. They asked, "Even if he prays and fasts?" He said, "Even if he prays and fasts and claims to be a Muslim. So call the Muslims by the names Allah gave them: the Muslims, the believing servants of Allah." This is a ḥasan hadith, and its words "Allah created you and sustains you, so worship Him and associate nothing with Him" are exactly the argument of these two verses.

### Oneness as the ground of peace

Tawḥīd, the most fundamental doctrine of Islam, is not a mere theory. It is the only effective way of making a human being truly human, his first and last refuge and the cure for all his ills. Its essence is that every change the physical universe can undergo, down to its own birth and death, hangs on the will of the One Being and displays His wisdom. When this doctrine takes hold of a person's mind and heart and becomes his settled state, all inner conflict stops and the world turns into a paradise for him, because he knows that the enmity of an enemy and the love of a friend both proceed from Allah, who rules both their hearts. Such a man lives in perfect peace. He fears no one and expects nothing from anyone. Heap gold on him or clap him in irons and he is unmoved, because he knows where each comes from. This is the meaning of the basic declaration of the creed, that there is no god but Allah. Saying it is not enough. One must have complete certainty and keep the truth always close to the heart, because tawḥīd is seeing Allah as one, not just saying so. Today the number of people who repeat the formula runs to millions, more than ever before, yet for most of them it is only breath spent. The colour of tawḥīd does not show in their lives. Otherwise they would be like their forefathers, whom neither wealth nor power daunted and neither numbers nor pomp overawed into turning their backs on the truth, when a prophet could stand alone against the world and say, "Call upon your associate-gods and conspire against me without delay" (7:195). If the Companions and their successors came to dominate the world within a few years, the secret lay in tawḥīd rightly understood and practised. May Allah grant all Muslims this great gift.

### The inner reading

Worship is bringing oneself into harmony with the command and pouring all one's energy into seeking the realisation of the unseen. The declaration of oneness enters through the heart, detachment through the innermost self, single-mindedness through intention, and humility through the self. Surrender is to the decree. It is also said: worship Him by renouncing what is forbidden, persevering in acts of obedience, welcoming the obligatory acts with humility and lowliness, and avoiding detours through the way-stations of laziness and indifference. The real meaning of taqwā, mindfulness of Allah, is protecting oneself, by conforming to His command, from the threats of punishment.

### In short

- "Worship your Lord" is addressed to everyone, and says something different to each: turn, be sincere, repent, persevere.
- The name Rabb carries the proof inside the command. The One who brought you from nothing and nurtures you is the only One worthy of worship, as the gravest sin is to set up an equal to Him who created you.
- "Those before you" makes Him the Creator of all mankind, and the silence about "those after you" hints that no community follows this one.
- "So that you may" expresses salvation as a hope, because Paradise is Allah's grace, not a wage. And tawḥīd, truly held, is the deepest peace a human being can have.

22.text:
The argument moves from the human self to the world around it. "˹He is the One˺ Who has made the earth a place of settlement for you and the sky a canopy; and sends down rain from the sky, causing fruits to grow as a provision for you. So do not knowingly set up equals to Allah ˹in worship˺". Verse 21 spoke of Allah's blessings in your own being. This verse speaks of His blessings in your surroundings. A human being has two dimensions, the inner, anfus, and the outer, āfāq, so between them the two verses sum up every kind of blessing that comes down on a person from Allah, and the conclusion follows: do not set up rivals to the One who did all this.

### Phrase by phrase

**"˹He is the One˺ Who has made the earth a place of settlement for you"** means He made it a bed to rest on, a place for dwelling and sleeping, like a carpet laid out, stable with the firm mountains. It is neither soft and fluid like water, on which nothing can settle, nor hard like stone or steel, which would be difficult to put to use, but a middle state between soft and hard, convenient for daily life. The word firāsh, bed, literally means something spread out. This does not deny that the earth is round. The great globe, round as it is, looks flat to anyone standing on it, and the Qur'an's way is to describe things as they appear to an ordinary person, literate or not, townsman or villager.

**"and the sky a canopy"** means a ceiling, a roof raised high above, an ornamented and beautiful one, masterfully built. Allah said elsewhere, "And We have made the sky a well-protected canopy, still they turn away from its signs" (21:32).

**"and sends down rain from the sky"** means through the clouds, when people need it. Water coming "from the sky" does not mean it falls without the medium of clouds. In everyday speech anything that comes down from above is said to come from the sky, and the Qur'an itself speaks several times of water sent down from the clouds: "Is it you who bring it down from the clouds, or is it We Who do so" (56:69), and "and sent down from rainclouds pouring water" (78:14).

**"causing fruits to grow as a provision for you"** means that by the rain He brings out every kind of vegetation and fruit as sustenance for people and their animals, a bounty the Qur'an mentions again and again. A similar verse reads, "It is Allah Who made the earth a place of settlement for you and the sky a canopy. He shaped you ˹in the womb˺, perfecting your form. And He has provided you with what is good and lawful. That is Allah—your Lord" (40:64). The repeated lesson is that Allah is the Creator, the Sustainer, the Owner and the Provider of this life and everything in it, so He alone deserves worship and nothing is to be associated with Him.

**"So do not knowingly set up equals to Allah ˹in worship˺"** means do not set up partners in worship, and do not say that Allah has peers, likenesses or equals, when you know that He fashioned all these things, that He is the Creator and you create nothing, and that only the One who creates can be God. It is also said that "knowingly" means: when you know from your own scripture that Allah has no son, no equal and no peer. The verse ends this way to rescue people from slavery to everything other than Allah.

### Four things no creature can do

The verse names four qualities of Allah that cannot possibly be found in a created being. The first three, the earth, the sky and the rain, belong to an order where human effort, human action and even human existence play no part whatever. Man did not yet exist when the earth and sky were already there and the clouds and rain were already doing their work, and not even a fool could imagine that these were the work of a man, an idol or any created being. The fourth, bringing out fruit and making it nourishment, is different. A simple person, looking at the surface, might credit it to human effort and ingenuity, because he sees people digging the earth, sowing seed and protecting the plants. But the Qur'an makes it plain that human effort has nothing to do with the actual growing of trees and the bringing out of fruit. All that human activity does is remove hindrances to a plant's birth and growth or protect it from being destroyed. Even the water that feeds the plant is not the farmer's creation. He only brings it to the plant at the right time and in the right amount. The birth and growth of the tree and the putting out of leaves, branches and fruit are the work of divine power and of no one else: "Have you considered what you sow? Is it you who cause it to grow, or is it We Who do so" (56:63-64). The only answer anyone can give is that Allah alone makes things grow.

Once these two verses have taught that Allah, and no one else, brings a human being out of nothing and provides for him by means of earth, sky, rain and fruit, anyone with a little common sense must admit that Allah and no one else deserves all worship and obedience. The ultimate wrong is to turn away from the One who gave you existence and the means of living and growing, and to prostrate yourself before others as helpless as you are. Allah placed man above all His other creatures so that the universe would serve him while he devoted himself wholly to worshipping, remembering and obeying Allah without distraction. Yet some people are so sunk in laziness and ignorance that they forget the One God, and in consequence end up serving a billion gods. Once one has understood that Allah alone is the Creator and the Provider, one has also understood that no one else can deserve worship or be set beside Allah as an equal or rival. These two verses call people to the essential purpose of every revealed Book and every prophet: tawḥīd, the affirmation and the worship of the one God.

### The signs of the Creator

Several scholars, among them ar-Rāzī, used these verses as a proof of the Creator's existence, and it is a most worthy line of argument. Whoever reflects on the things that exist, the higher creatures and the lower, their varied shapes, colours, habits, benefits and roles, comes to recognise the power, wisdom, knowledge, perfection and majesty of their Creator. A bedouin asked for evidence of Allah's existence replied: praise be to Allah, camel droppings point to a camel and footprints point to someone walking, so does a sky holding the giant stars, a land with its open roads and a sea with its waves not point to the existence of the Most Kind, the All-Knowing? Whoever gazes at the sky in its vastness and at the planets in it, some of which seem fixed in place, at the seas surrounding the land on every side, at the mountains set on the earth to steady it so that its inhabitants of every shape and colour can live and thrive, whoever reads the verses about the mountains with their streaks of white, red and raven black, and people, living creatures and cattle of as many colours, ending "Of all of Allah's servants, only the knowledgeable ˹of His might˺ are ˹truly˺ in awe of Him" (35:27-28), whoever considers the rivers running from land to land bringing benefit, and the animals and plants of every taste, scent, shape and colour that spring from the meeting of earth and water, knows that all of this testifies to the existence of the Creator and to His perfect power, wisdom, mercy, kindness, generosity and compassion toward His creation. There is no god but Allah and no Lord besides Him. On Him is our reliance and to Him is our return in repentance. The Qur'an has many verses on this theme.

### Seeing through the causes

Tawḥīd has an all-pervading and radically transforming effect on every sphere of life, inner and outer, individual and collective. Once a person believes that a single Being is the universe's Creator, Lord and Master, that He alone holds all power and decrees even the smallest atom's slightest movement, and that without His will no one can harm or help anyone, that person, rich or poor, in joy or sorrow, looks only toward that One Being and gains the insight to see, behind the veil of apparent causes, the working of the same omnipotence. If the modern worshippers of "energy" understood tawḥīd at all, they would see at once that power lives neither in steam nor in electricity, and that every power comes from the One Being who created both. Seeing this takes insight. The greatest philosopher in the world, if he misses this truth, is no better than the rustic who saw a train move when a green flag was waved and stop when a red one was waved, concluded that the flags controlled the huge machine, and bowed to them. People laugh at him because he does not know that the flags are only signals and the train is run by the driver, or better, by the engine. A more perceptive observer credits the steam inside the engine. The believer in one God laughs at all these wise men, because he sees through the steam, the fire and even the water to the might of the One Being who created fire and water and whose will makes them do their appointed work.

### Why people worship what they can see

Allah alone created mankind and everything in the heavens and the earth. He invested the world with deep meaning and constantly tends its needs. The right course for a human being is to take Allah as his Creator, Master and Sustainer and to set no partner beside Him, that is, to give himself up wholly to Allah. But because Allah is unseen, it often happens that a person gives weight to some visible thing and worships it instead. He equates the created with the Creator, sometimes a part of creation and sometimes creation as a whole, sometimes calling it God and sometimes not. This is man's basic error. The prophets taught people to glorify Allah alone and abandon the other things they had raised to glory. People whose hearts are attached to things other than Allah find the call of true religion repellent. They have grown so attached to their supposed deities that they cannot believe they are unreal, and they cannot believe that the truth is what a mortal like themselves proclaims.

### The inner reading

Earth and sky are full of wonders of power and marvels of wisdom, and these are evidence of a Lord and Creator, witnesses to His oneness, His knowledge and His power. He set the seven green domes upon the wind, one above another, without pillar or joint, as a mark of His power, and set the seven dust-coloured hills upon the water as a display of His wisdom. Of the one He says, "Indeed, We have placed constellations in the sky, and adorned it for all to see" (15:16), and of the other, "As for the earth, We spread it out. How superbly did We smooth it out" (51:48). Consider the likeness of two doves, one black and one white, flying within the blue dome. On the wings of one is written "We made the sign of the night devoid of light" and on the wings of the other "We made the sign of the day ˹perfectly˺ bright" (17:12). The black is born from the white and the white appears from the black: "He wraps the night around the day, and wraps the day around the night" (39:5), "Allah causes the night to merge into the day, and the day into the night" (22:61). Pure and faultless is the God who brings the brightness of day out of the pitch-black night and makes the darkness of night appear out of the brightness of day. More wondrous still, He placed the brightness of knowing at the centre of the heart's dark blood and the brightness of seeing at the centre of the eye's black pupil. By this you know that He is the perfectly powerful, the generous and bountiful giver. The bright day is the sign of the covenant of good fortune, and the dark night the likeness of days of trial, as if to say: you who enjoy the ease of daylight, do not feel secure, for the darkness of trial's night follows on its tracks.

### In short

- Earth as a bed, sky as a roof, rain from above and fruit from the ground: four blessings that no creature could produce and that no one was present to witness being made.
- Even the fourth, the harvest, is Allah's work. The farmer only clears the way; the growing is His.
- These verses are a proof of the Creator from the order and variety of creation, and the believer learns from them to see Allah's power behind every apparent cause.
- The conclusion is the verse's own command: knowing all this, set up no equal to Allah, whether a visible idol, a force of nature, or anything else the heart clings to.
